electing me as president for this 30th session. is truly an honor for me, from uganda, a land locked state, to assume this responsibility at a pivotal at such a pivotal moment for the international seabed authority, the international seabed authority and the resources there in a common heritage of all humankind.; yet to the extent that the international area lies beyond the reach of all states, we are all land locked states.; delegates, members of the council and esteemed representatives of the international sea bed authority. we are gathered here, not only as representatives of our nations, but as custodians of the shared of a shared global responsibility, the stewardship of the sea bed, which is a designated which is designated as a common heritage of mankind. our task ahead of us is both complex and significant, and i'm confident that together, we will continue the important work of this council in a spirit of cooperation and shared purpose. as a firm believer in multilateralism, i think that all members should aim to negotiate in good faith and in the spirit of compromise to ensure that we adopt the regulations. must be proud of our efforts at the authority over the past 30 years, where we have witnessed transparency in the conduct of our work, where non member states and other observers have been allowed to participate in the deliberations of the council, based on my several years in my throttle diplomacy, this is even more so here than at any other international governmental organizations. i intend to have an open door policy and meet with members of the council individually, as well as with small groups in order to resolve outstanding issues. overthe years, once again, delegations have demonstrated a strong commitment to advancing the negotiations on the draft exploitation regulations. it is imperative that we maintain this commitment negotiating in good faith is a constructive approach that ensures tangible progress. our mandate is clearly established in the convention and in the 1994 agreement, and we must remain faithful to these foundational instruments as we work towards a fair and effective mining port, the road map endorsed by the council provides us with a structured framework to advance our work we must continue to build on the progress made, ensuring that the legal, technical and environmental aspects of deep sea mining are addressed comprehensively and responsibly. successful conclude. successful conclusion of these negotiations is not merely an institutional goal. it is a necessity to provide clarity, legal certainty and a balanced regulatory framework that benefits all complexity of our discussions necessitates continued engagement in the intersessional work of the informal groups. these groups play a very important role in deepening our understanding of key issues, bridging divergent views and refining text of the regulations. i encourage all delegations to remain engaged in these processes and to approach our deliberations with the flexibility and pragmatism required to reach consensus this at the same time, i urge all participants to uphold the principles of dialog, inclusivity and transparency. let us be mindful that obstructionism serves no one. rather, it undermines the very foundation of multitasking. we must ensure that our legislative work moves forward in a timely and effective manner, respecting the efforts made by all stakeholders to arrive at balanced and fair outcomes. world is watching our work, our ability to demonstrate unity, determination and a commitment to sustainable and equitable management of seabed resources will be a testament to the strength of international cooperation. let us therefore move forward with purpose, the spirit of consensus building and with a shared vision for the responsible development of this common heritage of mankind, look forward to working closer with you all the coming days and weeks together. let us make this session a productive and meaningful one. i thank you.

column5: mr. president, i will refer here to your consultation on the use of severe harm or harmful effects. for my delegation, this shouldn't even be a matter of debate. there are many lawyers present among us here, and all lawyers can be clear that we should not substitute the term harmful effects for serious harm. these are two in legal terms. these are two different terms with different meaning, and are treated differently in unclos and this should be reflected similarly in the regulations, as the context would require in the context in which we are making a reference in the preamble, the context requires the use of harmful effects, because we're talking about the reference made in article 145 which ensures an effective connection of the against harmful effects that could be derived from activities in the area that this is the application of the obligation of all member states to protect and preserve the marine environment. article 192 of unclos also states that we should establish norms, regulations and procedures to reduce and control contamination of the marine environment from the activities in the area. these are affirmative obligations imposed by unclass and there is no there's no reference to here, to serious harm, but to harmful effects. serious harm is the extreme case, only in specific cases, and should not be the reference point used for the general obligations for environmental protection of articles 145, 192 and 209, these are express general obligations. this should be reflected in the not only in the preamble, but throughout the regulations. for example, in part 11, there's a specific reference to emergency orders to suspend activities in the area and for the designation of prohibited areas in which activities will not be allowed. as is noted, we should use the term harmful effects. thank you very much. applause.

column5: my second point we wish to comment on the first sentence of the second paragraph, which reads that the objective of the regulations is to regulate the exploitation of, quote, mineral resources of the area. unquote to us, this immediately highlights the importance of the schedule. term mineral resources is not defined in the schedule. only defined term that is close to giving us some guidance here on the interpretation of the term resources is the term resources and that is defined as referring to all solid, liquid or gaseous mineral resources, mineral bearing or associated mineral or a mixture thereof, in situ, in the area at or beneath the seabed. and to us, this immediately puts in question the exact scope of the draft regulations. the preamble could be read as implying that the regulations pertain to more resources than just polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulfides and cobalt rich ferro manganese crusts the kingdom of the netherlands questions whether this is our intention. would be beneficial to clarify this point specifically note that it may be undesirable to have these exploitation regulations regulate beforehand in all resources, whatever they encompass, indeed, even the exploration regulations only deal with the three resource categories i just mentioned.; the kingdom of the netherlands observes that certain parts of the regulations would have to be drafted in such manner they're actually resource specific. now, according to our analysis, this, in any event goes for the regulations and standard and guidelines on and i list environmental environmental impact assessments, environmental impact statements, environmental management and monitoring plans, mining closure plans, environmental studies, all the guidelines for baseline environmental data, environmental thresholds, and the financial term of contract. we intend to further discuss these differences when negotiating these respective topics. as a consequence, the kingdom of the netherlands is of the opinion that the council should clarify the scope of the draft regulations. the council should therefore scrutinize the exploitation of each respective resource separately, as opposed to mineral resources in a broad sense, as included in the preamble. now, as such, the preamble should make explicit which resources we now seek to regulate, seeing as much labor will have to be expended to account for the resource category in question.; on the numerous items we just listed, the kingdom of the netherlands considers that it might expedite the current negotiations if the council were to focus on one resource category only, recall that article 162 paragraph two, sub o roman two unclos provides that priority should be given to the adoption of rules, regulations and procedures for the exploration for and exploitation of poly metallic nodules. along that reasoning, we suggest that the draft regulations for the time being focus on poly metallic nodules.

column5: ireland fully agrees that proposals should not be included in the draft text where they are clearly inconsistent with the convention and the agreement. for this reason, we want to express our considerable disappointment and frustration with the continued inclusion of serious harm as a general standard for harm in the revised consolidated text, as the commentary notes, this is a cross cutting issue. serious harm is used in the convention in very specific and clearly defined contexts. first, it is the threshold for the council to issue emergency orders under article 162 for the ltc to recommend such as under article 165 secondly, it is the threshold for the council to disapprove areas for exploitation under article 162 and for the ltc to recommend the disapproval of areas under article 165 thirdly, and finally, it is the threshold for a court or tribunal to issue provisional measures under article 290 general standard for the harm threshold in the context of the rrps is very clearly defined. article 145 provides that necessary measures shall be taken in accordance with this convention with respect to activities in the area to ensure effective protection for the marine environment from harmful effects may arise from such activities. to this end, the authority shall adopt appropriate rules, regulations and procedures. moreover, under our under annex three of the convention, article 17 provides rules, regulations and procedures shall be drawn up in order to secure effective protection of the marine environment from harmful effects directly resulting from activities in the area. there is simply no tenable legal case to be made for the inclusion of serious harm in place of harmful effects as a general standard. such a proposal is clearly inconsistent with the convention. this is a significant issue in a long list of unresolved regulatory matters. it is, in fact, a very legally straightforward matter, and one that we should be able to agree on and cross off the list.

will not only shape the present, but define the future for generations to come. in regards to the preamble text that the area and its resources are the common heritage of humankind, exploitation should be carried out for the benefits of humankind as a whole, i'd like to take this moment to reiterate we are gathered here under mandate that carries extraordinary responsibility to act on behalf risk creating irreversible environmental consequences and undermining the very common heritage principle that the isa was established to protect questions for us remain unanswered, like, how do we define acceptable environmental harm when scientific understanding is complete, incomplete. how do we guarantee that irreversible environmental consequence consequences are not imposed on future generations yet to be born? and how do we ensure intergenerational equity risks are imposed today without mechanisms to account for long term consequences. if we are to uphold our duty as stewards of the seabed, for the common heritage of humankind and to mine future generations, the isa must first ensure that science, not commercial urgency dictates the way forward. the impact of decision today will not be measured in the coming years, but will be measured by many future generations to come. this is what here today to make sure our perspective is heard and taken into account, because the obligation to protect the marine environment under unclos thus and should not start after regulations are in place. it must be a requisite to any discussion on exploitation and exploration, please truly uphold the principle of common heritage of humankind. we must first ensure that we do no harm. thank you.

column5: since the terms harmful effect been discussed today, we would like to remind the council that the definition of the definition of harmful effects and the definition of serious harm have not been adequately addressed and discussed by the council. what we will need are specific criteria to operationalize measure and monitor both terms, given that the prevention of harmful effect is the overall objective and the term serious harm is used in the context of emergency measures and for pausing seed mining, seabed mining. we would like to stress that the definitions of both terms must be resource ecosystems and area site specific, an area and site specific because different deep sea environments and ecosystem have different characteristics and requirements.; because of this complexity, we would like to suggest a broad, thorough discussion, intersessionally, for instance, in the form of a workshop to define both terms harmful effects and serious harm, and to address this their operationalization do see as an international network of deep sea scientists and other experts stand ready to assist in this matter.

we are concerned that there's a desire to exclude parts of the convention specifically part 12, as the preamble states to these regulations that are being negotiated, these regulations are in accordance with the convention and in keeping with part 11. and at no point are we saying that this is in keeping with part 11 of the convention. so we consider that the regulations must take into account all of the convention, and not only part 11, as in the case of part 12. so in regards to the comments that we have, we support the views expressed by the delegation of costa rica, and in keeping with what portugal said one, this should be kept in terms of general policy. and so we ask that this be included in the next version or draft of the text. in regards to paragraph three, we consider it important that these also be mentioned. in particular, alt three is the one that best reflects us. why is this so, mr. president? because when we consider that the preservation of the common heritage of humankind is at stake. we're talking about humankind itself. so these regulations are not something that can be negotiated from in an isolated manner, from the international processes that we are developing in our own states, there is a context this has to do with the future mineral exploitation of the marine sea beds. so it's important that these are the principles that govern these activities, and that we consider all of the important aspects for these activities, in keeping with part 11, but also other international agreements and the international frameworks that have given us directives and objectives that we must follow. so this cannot be done in an isolated manner from the global objectives that we are to follow to ensure the health of oceans, the environmental health and that of the world for future generations. for this reason, we think it's very important to include all of these aspects in the principles that will govern these regulations.

column4: on article 145a in unclos: if mining code is weaker it may face legal challenges; on ecological balance and ecosystem integrity
column5: thank you, mr. president, for giving me the floor and good afternoon to the meeting. since it is the first time we speak, we would like to congratulate you for your election, and of course, congratulate again the new secretary general for her election. we also acknowledge with thanks, the emphasis she made on inclusiveness and transparency as well as the importance of the rule of law. the isa is an exceptional and remarkable institution of international law that we hope to see strengthen and succeed in fulfilling its dual mandate of regulation and control and protection of the marine environment. we are looking forward to supporting the work of this body in the development of robust exploitation regulation, implementing on clause and international law in general, as well as sound science and the best available technology. on behalf of a cops the advisory committee on protection of the sea, a charitable organization composed primarily of academic experts from different continents and islands, i would like to return to a point we have made before, and in several occasions we highlighted a part of article 145 that has not been discussed much, though it needs implementation in the new regulations that are being developed. we are referring to article 145 a on the adoption of rules and regulations and procedures to be adopted by the authority to prevent, reduce and control interference with the ecological balance of the marine environment, a subset in the development of rules that must be adopted to ensure effective protection of the marine environment from harmful effects from activities in the area. many delegations yesterday already referred to the importance of article 145 in guiding the development of the new body of regulations now being negotiated, it is indeed essential that these regulations comply with the convention. they can do more, but cannot do less without exposing the new regulations to legal challenges. we noted that the interference with the ecological balance is mentioned once in the current text in square brackets in regulation 44 however, it seems to us that it also has its place along the protection of biodiversity and ecosystem integrity, mentioned in this regulation, in paragraph two of this regulation, too, we note the protection of biodiversity and ecosystem integrity and agree that they are critical as components of the marine environment. there we would like to highlight that it is not only included as an objective in the global biodiversity framework, but also in the preamble of the bbnj agreement, as well as in a number of other recent instruments adopted under the auspices of global and regional legal agreements and frameworks on the protection of the marine environment. however, ecosystem integrity is not ecological balance. it is at most a proxy for the non interference with the ecological balance of the marine environment. much science is still needed to get to adequately understand this concept of ecological balance of the marine environment. but this concept is the language of article 145 itself, and therefore a binding objective that dates back from 1982 it therefore has its rightful place in the environmental principles and approaches in this regulation too. we hope that these comments are helpful and can be put to good use. thank you.

column4: response to russia on intergenerational equity
column5: amahilu, thank you, mr. vice president. for giving me the floor. wilkes gwyneth. melissa wi i am a member of wealth gwyneth, of the gig sand nation located in canada. gwyneth is our hereditary chief, and i am giving this intervention on behalf of the sustainable ocean alliance. we support the interventions from the federated state of micronesia, maui, nui, makai network and our other pacific partners who spoke before us on dr two and specifically in response to russia's comment on intergenerational equity. intergenerational equity is a well established concept and a core principle of the united nations. it is well defined. the principle of intergenerational equity recognizes the rights of each generation to use and enjoy the natural resources of the planet, and the corresponding duty to conserve these resources for the future. as the purpose of this exercise is to ensure the deep sea is for the benefit of humankind. we reject the proposal to remove the concept of intergenerational equity. additionally, today and yesterday, there have been many interventions about the need to align the regulations more closely with unclos. i would like to draw attention to article 140 and unclos, which states that particular consideration should be given to those who have not attained full independence or other self governing status. this includes indigenous peoples. it is important to note that the gigs and nation has never ceded our territory, and this was recognized by the supreme court of canada. so this point is pertinent to the gigs and nation and to other indigenous peoples in this room and beyond. it seems in these proceedings that there is often particular consideration given to the interest and timeline of mining corporations, instead of those who have not yet attained their full independence. if we are to fulfill the mandate of the isa to care for the seabed for the benefit of humankind, how can we do this when we have not specifically included the peoples who have the longest relationship with the ocean, when states are debating the very inclusion of future generations and indigenous rights in this section on guiding principles, as we discussed dr two, the mining code and also the role of the isa more broadly, it is essential to meaningfully include indigenous people for three reasons. first, indigenous peoples have a unique cultural relationship to the ocean that must be integrated into our understanding and definition of our common heritage. second, indigenous peoples have 1000s of years of expertise on the marine environment and should be included in the scientific understanding of impacts on deep sea mining. thirdly, many countries here have ratified the un declaration on the rights of indigenous people and have the responsibility to conduct free, prior and informed consent with their indigenous populations on the impact of deep sea mining. how many countries have properly conducted this? we must ensure that the regulations we are writing are aligned with undrip and that this process is supported by the principles of undrip, we therefore support the text of 4h with the deletion of where available. and thank canada and other states for also supporting this. lastly, i respectfully request that the isa and its member states fulfill these obligations and give special consideration to indigenous peoples in these proceedings. what does special consideration include? i would like us to start by asking the isa to create a fund to ensure the participation of indigenous peoples in this process, including these meetings, the ltc and the intersessional working groups. the section on underwater, underwater cultural heritage is essential, but it's not the indigenous section of the regulations. this must be integrated throughout the entirety of the isa has a responsibility to all of humankind and a special responsibility to those seeking independence and those unable to represent themselves agreements and organizations and the duty to cooperate. our impression is that council members sometimes recognize this, for example, with the precautionary approach, but other times seem oddly resistance, resistant to look beyond uncles part 11, for example, when it comes to biodiversity, human rights or climate change, we urge member states individually to continue to raise all global column5: thank you, mr. president, this intervention is on behalf of the deep sea conservation coalition and greenpeace international, and we would also like to express our support for the interventions of our colleagues amongst the observers who have just spoken. principles serve as the foundation for the regulations. they are broad, universal and timeless guidelines that help inform and shape decision making and behavior regarding the substance of dr two, we support the content of paragraph, alt, three, alt, including the wording on biological diversity and ecosystem integrity. we think this dr still does not sufficiently reflect other current, fundamental and globally agreed principles and commitments to not only protect and preserve but to halt and reverse or otherwise prevent biodiversity loss, to prevent the degradation of marine ecosystems, to protect and restore the health productivity and resilience of oceans and marine ecosystems, and to build ocean ecosystem resilience, all of these being textual key elements of the 2012 rio plus 20 outcome document the future we want the 2030 sustainable development. gold 14, target two, the bbnj agreement, as well as the marine and coastal decision adopted by cbd cop 15 in 2022, and the global biodiversity framework.; we support the interventions of brazil, costa rica, portugal, panama, switzerland and others on the need to retain in paragraph three a, the requirement to adopt an environmental policy and a number of the proposals from the african group chile, the netherlands, australia, ireland and others on the need to strengthen the environmental provisions in this dr, like brazil, belgium and others, we hope to see the development of a general policy for the protection and preservation of the marine environment by the assembly of the isa; in addition, whilst dr two includes a requirement for the use of relevant traditional knowledge of indigenous peoples in local communities, and we would agree with costa rica to remove where relevant, it fails to incorporate the duty to safeguard and protect indigenous cultural values and to obtain the free prior and informed consent of indigenous peoples and local communities potentially affected by decisions of the authority. nor does it include a fundamental principle, which we see as important, under which the isa would be required to obtain a broader understanding of the role of the deep sea in regulating global planetary processes through dedicated marine scientific research before any applications for plans of work are considered.; in summary, all of the above reflect clear, fundamental global commitments states have already made over the past two decades or so, which are of great importance to civil society and the future of our planets. states should insist that these be recognized and adhered to by the isa, amongst other potential impacts, scientists have highlighted the risk of driving species extinct, including species that may not yet have been discovered or described for the isa to authorize nodule mining in the full knowledge of this risk, but without understanding how to prevent it, nor establishing an obligation to do so, would be gambling with numerous environmental risks, including species extinctions that a global regulatory body of 169 countries in the european union responsible for managing seabed activities across half the surface of our planet would knowingly and willingly authorized nodule mining under these circumstances should be unthinkable. doing so would risk turning the clock back on, involving international commitments to conserve biodiversity, protect the environment and pursue sustainable development by 2030, or maybe 50 years, and to paragraph the name of the rio plus 20 outcome document is this, or would this be, really be the future we would want? thank you.

in any case, if this is damages to the environment, then in the regulations, we have many other tools to deal with such damages. we have the environmental performance guarantee, we have insurance available and so on. also, if, after the deliberations, a decision is taken to retain this responsibility of the parent company, then perhaps we need to talk about subsidiary responsibility and not joint and several liability. point three, with regard to regulations and applicable standards, we should use the phrase in accordance with and as far as guidelines and ramps are concerned, we need use, we should use the risk taking into account, with regard to three, b's two, 3b, c2, i think it's enough to make a reference to regulation 48 terror it may happen when carrying out some additional test mining is not necessary because they are using exactly the same technology and the same conditions, but but regulation 48 terror shall describe such instances. the following remark refers to three, b's, d, bid, so perhaps a test mining study, prepared, prepared if necessary, or it may be based on some other document in accordance with regulation 48 terror, another document means that a test mining is not submitted, but what they submit is another document that justifies the current situation. now h we agree with this concise wording that we currently see, and we would like to say that the environmental management and monitoring plan already assumes, as some regulations have some provisions from the ramps, and also includes a description of an environmental management system as regulation 52.2 says that such system is present in detail as part of the ramp. also we agree the deletion of sub paragraph k as we see it here. thank you.

column4: 3 bis d bis should be report not study; in case of existing technology should be tested in similar environment
column5: thank you, mr. president, regarding paragraph 3d, d, bis, we're talking about here test mining study, and we believe that this should actually be a report and not a simple study. and then at the end of the paragraph, we consider that we should add validated by the isa in a sim in a similar geographic area. and be necessary that if we are going to accept mining tests, because other prior tests have showed that the techniques used are valid, we need to be clear that these are tests that are appropriate pertinent to the geology and the characteristics of the sea bed in question. and forgive me for going to entirely to another subject. but we would also like to support the request made by costa rica regarding the work on underwater cultural heritage, and congratulate also the work of our colleague from micronesia, who has worked on a work alone, has worked alone on a considerable subject that is of interest to all of us. thank you, mr. president.

column4: agrees with russia in what damages are being meant, thinks it should be environment, but want to keep it here for now until covered sufficiently elsewhere; 3 bis h and k, also wants to keep here for now
column5: thank you, mr. president, on paragraph 2d, i shared the same question as the russian federation on what like, what damages are we referring to here? what makes sense to me is that there would be damages to the environment. i understand also that there will be other instruments that will address this, but those instruments are still far from being clearly defined, in particular in terms of the coverage and the funding that will be available to address this, this liability. so for the time being, i would much prefer that to have it here, and then in the end, it will be easier to see if that will be addressed sufficiently by other instruments regarding paragraph three b's in subparagraph h and k, there's a question on the comments box that we should take into consideration keeping or or eliminating this, this, this language here, and for the time being, again, we would like to keep it here until we are sure about having these issues covered sufficiently, because these are both important topics from our perspective, to not lose sight of them. thank you.

column4: supports 2d that addresses corporate complexity; opposed to removing 2d; supports removing 3 bis "or will have" wording; concerned about elimination of 3 bis k; move part to reg 16
column5: panama supports the inclusion of paragraph 2d addressing the structural complexities of the corporate entities, and we believe it would be better to reformulate this provision to establish an obligation of presenting a declaration of financial responsibility by the parent company in keeping with the proposal of the netherlands, it is key that this mechanism not be limited only to the responsibility of the applicant before the international seabed authority, but that it also cover third party liability, including those of member states and other actors with legitimate interests in the marine environment. we need to consider that joint responsibility must go beyond a mere reparation of harm once these violations have taken place, and we should establish a means of guaranteeing actively that the contractor meet its contractual obligations within the applicable framework. we also support the inclusion of a clear definition agreed to by consensus regarding the parent company or the holding company, ensuring that these meet key requirements such as taking strategic decision, strategic decisions, being able to control the board of the contractor, the rights to vote, and any other form of substantial influence on the management and operation panama, as opposed to the elimination of previous paragraph 2d which requires contractors to meet with legislation and regulations of the sponsor state. it is fundamental that this maintain the improve the capacities of supervision of the authority. we also support the elimination of phrase three biz regarding financial and technical capacities. we believe applicants must show existing capacities in instead of future capacities in keeping with the qualifications of unclos. in this regard, we also want to express our concern about the elimination of paragraph three biz on corporate policies, the authority must have access to the internal governance framework of applicants to evaluate adequately their commitments to safety, ethics, ethics and responsibility. finally, we support the concept of staged decision making in the areas of mining, but we suggest repositioning these provisions in regulation 16 to make this clearer and more coherent thank you mr. president.

column4: proposed deletion of 2d, because parent and subcompanies are legally separate entities; references unclos; thinks it is covered elsewhere; 3 bis d bis china will address it when negotiations come to that
column5: china proposes the deletion of this paragraph on the following grounds, first, according to the prevalent corporate practice in the world, the parent and subsidiary companies are individual legal entities with distinct responsibilities, unless there is a legal situation under which company is to be unveiled, quote, unquote, the parent company should not undertake collateral responsibilities for the subsidiaries. act or non act i it the existing international resource development mechanisms. for example, the mechanism governing the development of oil and gas in the world normally does not require the parent company to bear the collateral responsibilities. secondly, and article, 139 of unclos, the tractors, should ensure that the sponsored contractor. the contracting parties should ensure that the sponsored contractor observes the obligations of the convention, but that's not extended to the parent company of the contractor. the parent company is not one that signs the exploitation contract. the requirement for the parent company to undertake the collateral responsibilities go beyond the framework of the convention. thirdly, in the existing draft regulations, there are already many provisions that serve as guarantee, for example, during the application stage, the assessment of the financial capabilities of the contractor and the contractors, insurance guarantee, financial guarantee for compliance and the environmental compensation fund, the monitoring obligations of the sponsoring state, etc. we should not have additional requirements by going beyond corporate laws and the convention. in future, we may as well further refine and improve the verification of the qualifications of the contractor to ensure its independent ability to bear the responsibilities as for the best and three best in this regulation, because it involves test mining. it's more closely related to 48 china will state is positioned when it's discussed in connection with article 48 i thank you mr. president.

column4: general comment on dsm, including science, uch, remps, etc; wants to keep "or will have" in 3 bis because of developing states; wants 3 bis d bis to be clear what test mining exceptions should be
column5: thank you, mister president. the kingdom of tonga welcomes important discussion on draft regulation seven form of applications and information to accompany a plan of work as a small state, tonga strongly supports a fair, efficient and predictable application that upholds the precautionary approach while ensuring environmental, social and cultural protections. otonga the ocean is not just a resource, it is our identity, heritage and way of life, any deep sea activity must integrate scientific best practices, precautionary approaches and traditional knowledge to safeguard marine ecosystem and the cultural values of pacific people. in this regard, the kingdom of tonga supports the alignment of applications with regional environmental management plans as a means to balance efficiency with environmental responsibilities ramps provides clear, structured and science based guidelines, ensuring that activities proceed with predictability and accountability while adhering to high environmental standards, we also support retaining the phrase i quote or will have end quote in regulation seven free bids to allow applicants to demonstrate access to financial and technical resources over time, requiring full resources up front could disproportionately impact developing states and sids, creating barriers to participation a flexible yet responsible approach ensures fairness without compromising regulatory integrity. additionally, while advancing in mining technology, may reduce the need for test mining. in some cases, any exemptions must be clearly defined to avoid weakening environmental safeguards, ensuring rigorous scientific validation before granting exemptions will maintain trust and transparency in the regulatory process. finally, the kingdom of tonga remains committed to gender equality, inclusivity and sustainability, responsible seabed mining must benefit all stakeholders equitably and protect the rights of future generations. the kingdom of tonga supports a balanced, precautionary and structured regulatory framework, one that ensures fair access, uphold environmental and cultural responsibilities and provide regulatory clarity for all stakeholders. we look forward to further constructive discussions on refining these regulations. i thank you, mr. president.

column4: 2b requires more consideration; 3 bis h acceptable with deletion; 3 bis k acceptable deletion
column5: thank you, mr. president, very quickly concerning para to the point of view this needs further consideration, as it is closely linked with the discussion on effective control, so we will need to get back to that. and para three b's h is acceptable to us with the current deletion, and three b's, k is accept the deletion is acceptable to us. thank you.

column4: supports keeping 2d on subsidiary companies; 3h should reference 50 not 48; 3j reference also wrong; supports canada and italy in deleting "or will have"; 3 bis k supports keeping it
column5: thank you. thank you, mr. president. and good morning all recalling our comments yesterday about the need to review provisions in the draft regulations regarding insurance and liability as a cross cutting issue. australia supports paragraph 2d being included in draft regulation seven. this will avoid the use of shell companies or subsidiary companies that are insufficiently financed, so as to limit or avoid liability by the contractor. we accept the comments of other delegations that this paragraph and some of the concepts it contains requires further elaboration to turn to a couple of editorial points, which i hope will be picked up at some stage, as i think the regulations will need what's called a legal scrub, or at least a thorough cross checking. we notice that in paragraph 3h the cross reference we think should be to draft regulation 50 not draft regulation 48 and similarly in paragraph 3j the reference to the application processing fee in appendix two needs checking, as appendix two is currently in the suspense document. we suggest this paragraph could be amended to say the application processing fee as decided by the council, with regard to the chapeau of what is now paragraph three, bis, we support panama and italy regarding the deletions of the words or will have, we think it's very important that the contractor have access to the necessary financial and technical capability and resources to carry out the proposed plan of work at the time the application is submitted. and finally, with regard to paragraph three, bis, subparagraph k, we support retaining this paragraph and the policy is referred to in it to inform the assessment process. thank you.

column4: 2d is important, one contract condition should be the respect of national rules, making it possibvle to states to regulate more effectively; wants to remove "or will have" in 3 bis, goes against unclos and should not encourage contractors to apply before they have the capabilities; 3 bis d bis supports panama and france; k should be kept; missing transfer of technology being mandatory, quotes unclos
column5: costa rica agrees with the addition to paragraph 2d this seems important to us, and we support it, however, we cannot support eliminating the previous paragraph 2d as mentioned by other delegations, this paragraph demanded that all contractors comply with the laws and regulations of the sponsoring state. for my delegation, if a contractor is not willing to respect the the the applicable national standards, we have a problem, and we should not approve a plan of work. it would also be good for the authority that one condition for the contract of the isa would be the respect of national rules. this would give us the possibility to adopt regulatory measures if national laws were not fulfilled, and not only in case of standards for the authority. so this would actually support the sponsoring states regarding paragraph three. bis, we support the delegations that were in favor of deleting or will have for my delegation. if we don't, we accept that the proof of technical and financial capability capacity be purely capability, be purely hypothetical at the time of the application, rather than a real proof of the capacity of the applicant, and this would go against the standards applied by unclos and the practice established in the exploration regulations as a matter of principle. moreover, we believe that we should not encourage contractors to request a contractor in the area unless they have real financial and technical capabilities to fulfill said plan of work regarding paragraph d in three. bis costa rica shares the comments made by panama, france and other delegations. we have stated that we are concerned by this additional text, and therefore we support the comments and suggestions of the distinguished ambassador from france regarding sub paragraph k costa rica does not agree with the deletion of this sub paragraph for the reasons already explained by other delegations, it seems very important to us to have a code of conduct. and even though there are there might be good will and best practices, we believe there should be a specific code of conduct in order that we could make sure that said code of conduct is fulfilled. and finally, mister president, we don't find on this list the the fact that the transfer of technologies is a mandatory issue. this despite the fact that in annex three of onclose, in articles 63 it is referred, and i quote to the commitments pertaining to the transfer of technology as a requirement for any application and prior requirement for the approval of a contract, and therefore it's important that this be included within this regulation. thank you very much.

column4: wants to clarify their stance on parent company liability; called for deletion of 2d because it is too weak, suggested multiple additions elsewhere; para 3 reference to remps, working group will commence after council meeting; 3bis delete or will have; 3 bis d bis new textual proposal together with ireland and should be read with 48ter
column5: mr. president, thank you for giving me the floor. i will provide the kingdom of the netherlands as comments on this draft regulation and immediately turn to paragraph two, sub d to just heard a reference to the kingdom of the netherlands's proposal on parent company liability statements. we take the floor to clarify that actually the kingdom of the netherlands submitted the textual proposal to delete this paragraph two sub d altogether. please allow me to explain, based on our national experience in the extractive industries, we are an avid proponent that parent companies of contractors should indeed be jointly and severably liable towards the authority. however, paragraph 2d was much too weak. the text of the draft as it previously stood, merely determines that the applicant will provide a written undertaking, that they will provide another written undertaking. this does not provide enough legal basis for such liability as such. we called for its deletion because the provision insufficiently covers a future contractor ensuring that its parent companies are jointly and severably liable. instead, last year, we submitted textual proposals to draft regulations. 18, bus 2324 annex nine or possibly 11. sorry, annex nine and the schedule, as well as a new annex 11, containing a statement through which parent companies of the contract agreed to such liability. these submissions should be read together. we're grateful for the initial positive response we received during the council second meeting of its 29th session in july last year. and look forward to further working with delegations on this important notion. we have listened carefully just now and taken notes of comments just voiced by other delegations. we will look forward to addressing any concerns going forward on paragraph three at the top, we note the input of a reference to ramps this paragraph, and is an example of what is to be discussed in the new intersessional working group. it is now our impression that the council is agreeable to this intersessional working group commencing and it being facilitated by the kingdom of the netherlands. i just wish to say that we intend to take up this work immediately after the first session of the council's 30th meeting, rather than prior to next week, friday for three bis we support the deletion of or will have specifically on paragraph three, bis, sub d. bis, we take note of the new textual proposal included in the consolidated version, which has a link to the proposals put forward by the kingdom of the netherlands and ireland on the assessment of mining technologies, and which was discussed during an informal lunch session last year, on the new textual proposal. we understand this should be read together with the new draft regulation 48 to alt and therefore consider it may be appropriate to discuss the concept put forward when the council negotiates that draft regulation. as these two notions are to be viewed holistically, just like china, we look forward to making advancement on this important topic when we arrive at that draft regulation 48 to alt and aligning regulation seven thereafter. thank you, mr. president.

column5: thank you, mister president. we have a very brief comment on para 2d to my delegation. this paragraph is important, but we support others view. for further elaboration of this paragraph, because it's in the region undertakings, we think that it should affirm the financial capacity of the parent or holding company, which is very important, and also that should include provisions for dispute resolution. we also see merit in china's comment on how we decide the responsibility of the parent company. we have also similar question raised by russia on damage. that is, what type of damage we are speaking here? is it environmental or third party claims or any other type of damage? thank you. we look forward to have a more elaborative paragraph in 2d for which would be agreeable to all of us. thank you.

column4: 2b supports china; wants to keep or will have, supports tonga
column5: thank you, mr. president, on draft regulation seven, we also express our concern on paragraph 2b for the reasons given by china and others and we and we recognize the need for further discussions on this. and we also support the intervention made by tonga on the issue over the proposal to remove the words or will have in three bits, we are concerned that this would remove the ability of applicants to demonstrate that they are capable of and will obtain the relevance capabilities and resources needed to carry out their plan of work. such an outcome would be overly restrictive for applicants, as it would require them to actually have, for example, significant funds on hand at the time of applying, rather than just demonstrating that they will have the relevant resources as needed throughout the life of their project.

column4: 2a supports, but should they reference guidelines?; 2d important, also liability statement from parent company; transfer of technology should be included; 3 bis d mining tech bracket part should be deleted; as france, study should be replaced with report
column5: turning first to the reference to guidelines in paragraph two a, as presently drafted, this would appear to make guidelines binding on the contractor, which presumably is not the intention we would accept a reformulation which requires contractors to undertake to take guidelines into account. we think new paragraph 2d is a step in the right direction to providing appropriate safeguards to ensure accountability and enforceability, as has already been pointed out, there was previously a proposal by the netherlands for a requirement to provide a parent company liability statement, which is something we would be in favor of, like others, we would also support the insertion of an additional requirement on an undertaking concerning the transfer of technology. this is a requirement under article six, three of annex three of undloss, with regard to paragraph three, bis d, bis ireland requests a deletion of the text in square brackets. we may understand the concept behind this, however, agreeing exemptions for test mining in regulation seven is premature. the concept of mature mining technology is also open to interpretation, and there is no reference to this term elsewhere in the regulations as the kingdom of the netherlands just mentioned it may be similar to proposals put forward on the assessment of mining technologies and how to use international standards in this regard, we therefore suggest this topic is further discussed when we reach reg 48 ter on test mining, at which point we will have a clear review on any exemptions that may be relevant and applicable. finally, as france suggested, we agree that the word study should be replaced with report, as is also described in regulation 48 sir. thank you, mr. president.

this issue, and we look forward to further discussions one para three in place of the phrase taking into account that is now used. germany believes that the wording, such as in accordance with or in conformity with, should be used it should be clear that there is no discretion for applicants in preparing the applications to regard ignore or contravene any of the instruments mentioned here. regarding para three biz, we support the deletion of the phrase four will have in the introductory paragraph. in our view, the applicant must already be in a position when submitting the application this information. hence, we could agree to adding the words, if any here, if that is helpful, in order to retain sub para k in the text, thank you, mister president.

column5: thank you very much, mr. president cuba supports the inclusion of paragraph 2d on paragraph three. bis we in agreement with the removal of the additional language that is bracketed, and we wish the requester to contain sufficient information to show that the requester has the sufficient financial and textual capacities to carry out the plan of work. we also include, we also support including within brackets, d bis, but we propose including the following text and that the requesters show that the technology used in the mining tests has been operational in areas with similar topographic and geologic conditions, then that the than that of the seabed for the request. thank you. thank you, tuba. i recognize spain.

column5: thank you, mr. president. with respect to paragraph 2d we have noted the positions of several delegations, and in particular, we thank the delegation of the netherlands for the additional explanation provided. nevertheless, we have several concerns and queries about this proposal, and consequently we look forward to further discussions on the matter. but subject to that, we reserve our position there on with respect to paragraph three base, we support the deletion of the phrase, or will have it is our delegations view that the applicant at the time of the application, should have the necessary financial and technical capacity and resources to carry out the program of of work. thirdly, we support the deletion of the words in brackets in our graph the 3d piece. thank you mr. president

column5: thank you, mr. president, and apologies if you'll allow a very brief comment to draft regulation six. first, as we did not get to comment on this yesterday, nowhere has doubts about the last part of draft regulation six. paragraph to this specifically if the content fits in this regulation and whether it is compatible with the convention and the 1994 agreement, as requested by you yesterday, mr. president, we will defer our comments to a later stage. for now, we reserve our position on this paragraph on draft regulation seven to paragraph one letter c norway agrees that we need management and monitoring regulation letter h also needs to be updated. norway would like to point out that currently draft regulation 52 paragraph one references the mentioning of environmental paragraph, updates and references and wording in light of the development of the regulations and definitions in the schedules are throughout this regulation. thank you.

column4: given chp the entire application should be published, not just environmental parts; aligns regulation with transparency principles; allows stakeholder consultations beyond environment; 2 bis simplified; 4 is more appropriate in dr12; welcomes further discussion on many paras
column5: thank you, mister president, for giving me the floor. this submission is made on behalf of the african group. the african group thanked the drafters for their hard work in consolidating the various comments from the previous version of this regulation. however, we believe that significant further refinements are needed to enhance transparency, streamline procedural efficiency and ensure consistency with the principles of common heritage of mankind. the african group strongly believe that the publication of an application should not be limited solely to environmental plans, given that resources in the area are the common heritage of mankind, the entire application should be available for consultation subject to appropriate reductions to protect legitimate commercial interests. thus, the african group recommend that the entire application be published with appropriate reduction to protect commercially sensitive information. stakeholder comments should not be restricted to environmental plans and non confidential parts of the test mining study, but should cover the entire application. this would align the regulation with transparency principles and allow for meaningful participation by all stakeholders, particularly those representing the interest of humanity. the african group believe that para paragraph should be simplified to strictly focus on the process for the secretary general to transmit comments received from stakeholders under regulation 93 bis to the commission. the commission should then consider this comments while fulfilling its duties under regulation 12. this adjustment would eliminate unnecessary procedural steps, making the review process more efficient while maintaining full transparency and stakeholder engagement. the african group agree with the substance of paragraph four, but believe it is more appropriately placed in regulation 12, which governs the commission's review process. this would improve the structural organization of the regulatory framework and ensure logical sequencing of procedures. the african group support the deletion of the bracketed portion of paragraph five, as is, provisions are already covered under regulation 12, retaining it would introduce unnecessary duplication, making the regulatory framework less efficient. the african group also acknowledged that this regulation may introduce additional procedural steps for the commission, potentially delaying the review and proceed the review and approval process. therefore, we are open to discussions on how to streamline the responsibilities assigned to the commission while maintaining robust environmental and procedural oversight. in this regard, the african group welcome further deliberations on paragraph 1235, excluding the bracketed portion and six to assess their procedural efficiency and operational feasibility. thank you mister president.

environmental plans, or can have indirect bearing on the environmental plans, also in sub paragraph 5b bis, there is reference to sub paragraph 1b of regulation 11. however, this sub paragraph does column5: thank you very much, mr. vice president, here there are comments that have already been made and allow us to limit our own intervention for costa rica, we find the alternative title preferable, not the original one, because there are other parts of a request that could contain information that is very relevant for the stakeholder consultation, for example, the mining plan or the financing plan. these could be very important for a review by stakeholders and particularly observers who are committed of when they apply, when these applications are made, i think it would be regrettable to limit these reviews to only environmental matters 14 countries, plus the entirety of the african union was were of this view last year. so i think that we should definitely go beyond just the mere environmental information. costa rica also supports the intervention of the african union regarding the importance of ordering a bit more this regulation in regard to the review procedure, because it seems to us that there are duplications here. the technical committee reviews this three times. it seems to us that it could be streamlined and better organized as the africa group, not the africa union, as the africa group has said, we also in agreement with the invention of the delegation of france with a preference for the use of report instead of study. with regards to test mining on three on point three quad, we've heard with attention the intervention of australia, and in effect, seven days may be too short a period of time to share the comments and have them published. so we are agree. we are in agreement that this period of time could be made a bit longer, not much, but the applicant should be timely advised if he needs to work on his requests further. as other delegations have already noted, we see two versions of paragraph five. my delegation supports five bis, as we believe it should be called, regulation five for costa rica is this paragraph five in the regulation is very important because we know that the technical committee meets twice a year. these are officers who are very dedicated to their work, but they have other responsibilities, and they will not necessarily have time to fulfill the heavy agenda of work that they have. and once the process of applications or requests begins, that work load will be even greater. and for this reason, it seems to us very important to be able to have recourse to outside experts. this is not something new. the etc, has been addressing this by having recourse to external experts for many years, the problem is that there was not a clear rule for the selection of experts. and my delegation, as others have already done, have been asking for a clear and transparent procedure as to what requirements should be met by experts, and how we avoid certain types of conflicts of interest, and that there be a geographical balance in terms of the nominations of such experts from my delegation. it is very important, then that we take the opportunity when there are these reiterated mentions in court, the experts are in are named and mentioned several times that we should also handle the process of the process of selection for costa rica. this should not be a guideline. it should be a standard or an annex that is incorporated into the regulations. in this sense, we have two options in paragraph five. one says may seek, and the other one says shall seek. but at the end of that paragraph, it also says, as necessary for my delegation, it would be very important. it is very important that the word use be shall. because what we are trying to say here is that when a when the etc determines that such expertise is not to be found within its own members, those etc members must not that they may, but that they must refer the matter to experts who have such expertise. that's why we will need to have the statement shall. but in the event that experts are not to be found within the etc, it is not it should not be optional to seek outside expertise, but rather that it be shall and not may, that's the position of costa rica. thank you very much

the commission has the appropriate means to perform the obligations that are placed on it in this regulation, nor further echoes others in streamlining the paragraph to eliminate duplication of reviews by the commission, specifically to the last sentence of paragraph one, if the commission shall review the comments from experts and provide comments of their own before the end of the scientific rigor, transparency and effective participation. we consider that the ter 11 limits consultation of environmental plans and the study or report from test mining, as others have stated, we analyze the comments to make its own assessment of the application, allowing the applicant to only sending on to the applicant only the elements that need further information. and as other delegations commission, as foreseen in articles 163 sub paragraph 13 and 173 sub paragraph 2e. of unclos we prefer as others, the formula may in this paragraph, since its grants the ltc autonomy to find external affect the process otherwise.

the bbnj agreement is a treaty that will cover numerous activities. it is aimed at achieving more holistic ocean governance by bringing together various regional and sectoral bodies to conserve and sustainably use marine biodiversity. by contrast, in these regulations, we are regulating a very specific activity pursuant to an exclusive mandate. so we are not sure that paragraph one four particularly appropriate in this context. it may give rise to legal uncertainty and could even risk lowering environmental standards in certain contexts. if there is a desire within the council to madam vice president.

column5: dosi, strongly supports the inclusion of the sufficient information requirement under para 1c, bis, the sufficient information refers to the level of knowledge required to make informed regulatory and management decisions and ensure adequate environmental protection and objectives for a particular site. the sufficiency criterion is not just about the quantity of data collected, though this is a relevant factor, but includes other factors such as data confidence and integrity and statistical power. the best available information may not always be sufficient to protect predict long term impacts of cbd mining activity or protect sea bed environments. effectively, the full meaning of sufficient information should be set out in a standard which can be cross referenced here as well in a defined term in the schedule, as a reminder, there are copies of doses policy brief on the sufficient information requirement outside. we also want to express our support for para 1c ter as deep sea science experts, we recognize the need to incorporate multiple knowledge systems, including indigenous and traditional knowledge. we also strongly support the inclusion of para 1h and the reference to climate mitigation and the ocean's capacity to function as a carbon sink. we support the inclusion of the reference to the ocean as a climate regulator, but would recommend maintaining the reference to carbon sink, particularly because of the obligation under article 4d of the united nations framework convention on climate change to conserve and enhance ocean sinks and marine ecosystems. a healthy ocean acts as the planets largest carbon sink, and its ability to moderate climate change decreases with disruption of marine systems. climate impacts of deep sea mining must be considered when assessing impacts, especially when considering whether deep sea bed mining benefits all of humankind on para one. i do see wants to again highlight, with regard to the mitigation hierarchy, that restoration is not currently known to be possible after deep sea bed mining activities first experiments on restoration in the deep sea are ongoing, but the results of these will take column5: thank you, mr. president, this intervention is on behalf of the environmental justice foundation, deep sea conservation coalition, oceans north, wwf international, maui, nui, maka network, greenpeace, the sustainable ocean alliance and the bucha society. we welcome the opportunity to comment on draft regulation 44 ter, concerning environmental goals and objectives. the provisions contained in article 44 ter are fundamental to integrating environmental protection elements into the structure and function of the isa without these provisions, the alignment between overall commitments and their practical application, risks being lost. scientists are warning of the severe and potentially irreversible risks posed by deep sea mining. these include the loss of genetic diversity, the disruption of population connectivity and the degradation of critical ecosystem functions, many of which remain poorly understood. all of these are issues drought regulation. 44 ter is trying to address. the deep ocean is one of the most fragile and least explored environments on the planet, it is imperative to ensure that the decision making process of the isa account for both the seriousness of these risks and the overwhelming scientific consensus calling for a precaution. it is therefore concerning that draft regulation 44 ter was deleted and moved to the suspense document, despite the fact that no explicit opposition on the content was raised during council discussions. on the contrary, the majority of states expressed support for the content and explicitly asked to retain this regulation in the draft, while a general policy to the same effect is developed. removing it now appears inconsistent with that direction and would undermine the authorities efforts to act in accordance with article 145 of unclos. we urge that draft regulation 44 ter on environmental goals and objectives be reinstated in the draft of the exploitation regulations, and we believe these goals and objectives should be reflected across all instruments of the isa, including in a general policy of the authority we consider its intentions to be central to the fulfillment of the mandate of the isa to protect the marine environment. thank you.

column5: mr. president, thank you for the floor and good morning to all many colleagues will know that, together with belgium and china, we have introduced a joint proposal on test and pilot mining during yesterday's informal session of the working group on test mining. today, i will therefore be very brief. the joint proposal is the result of very intense and constructive work between germany, belgium and china during the first two days of this week, we would like to use the opportunity to express our sincere gratefulness to our colleagues from belgium and china. from the beginning, there was broad agreement between our delegations about the concepts that there should be one phase of test mining during the exploration phase, and that there should be another phase of testing before commercial production can begin, in order to fully assess the environmental impact of commercial mining. we agree with china that it makes sense to call this second phase pilot mining, and we did so in our joint proposal. but just to make clear, the pilot mining during the exploitation phase is in essence what discuss, what was discussed, and also in the working group on test mining the joint proposal is a package we try to address all the provisions that relate to test and pilot mining. we put the proposal forward for the kind consideration of all delegations, and today we look forward to hearing some initial reactions. it is, however, our intention to continue the intersessional work on test and pilot mining to give every room possible for future discussions on this topic for this week, the co facilitators aim to organize another virtual meeting before the next council meeting, and thank you mr. president.

mining represent these things, but critical phases in the mining cycle. test mining is intended to validate the technical appropriateness of proposed mining equipment, while pilot mining serves to prove commercial and technical viability of the fully integrated mining system. both phases must include environmental monitoring of their impacts on the marine environment. the african group strongly supports the explicit retention of both regulation 48 ter and 48 ter alt, as proposed, given the respective roles in the mining, mining progression, this mining should remain a pre request for consideration of a plan for while pilot mining must be a requirement before any commercial production begins. we emphasize that test mining is not just a data collection exercise, but must validate african group considers that paragraph two of the regulation must clearly articulate this developed objective, this mining should inform and validate the environmental impact assessments and support the review of the plan of work for exploitation. pilot pilot mining shall confirm the commercial readiness and technical soundness of the integrated mining system. we underline that this validation activities on the marine environment. the african group supports incorporating clear criteria and standards defining the scale, duration, environmental objectives and monitoring frequencies of tests and pilot mining. this prevents any risk of test mining being used as distinguished as disguised pre exploitation. we further propose the regulation mandates a public, publicly available detailed guidelines, legal safeguard of must prevent test or pilot mining from becoming a pathway to commercial exploitation without oversight or royalty obligation. the african group stress the need to heritage principle. lastly, we strongly, we strongly. we strongly support a phased approach, a small scale but scientifically meaningful testimony phase before plan of work submission and the second column5: thank you, mr. president, and good morning colleagues, briefly, if i may, on the wider process, we concur that time should be taken to get this regime right. but if there is a vacuum, the isa should be putting in place a moratorium pause, rather than hastily rushing to conclude these regulations. turning to the test mining proposal, we thank the proponents for the new proposal and look forward to further engagement on this important topic once we have had the time to consider the implication and interactions with various parts of the regulations. and we found this initial discussion today and the answers to some of the questions helpful in this respect. in the meantime, we had two questions about the proposal. firstly, is test mining as defined in the proposal still a mandatory requirement before an application for a plan of work of exploitation? we think test mining should be mandatory prior to exploitation contract award to ensure the best possible evidence base for isa decision making without test mining under exploration, the isa will be receiving applications for exploitation based on conjecture, modeling and hypothesis, which is not a good basis for permitting a potentially hugely harmful new extractive industry. we take the opportunity in this regard to repeat a call we have made at every isa session for years now. the eia rules under exploration need to be improved and strengthened. the process set by the isa currently includes no screening, no scoping, no peer review, no expert review, apart from completeness and statistical reliability, inadequate consultation, and crucially, no permitting decision by the council. the rules for eia under exploration are set by the ltc, and have the ltc making decisions which is beyond their legal mandate, and specifically, they are tasked to take unilateral decisions about what levels of harm are acceptable without the council having established those parameters. unless the eia rules under exploration are reformed, the isa does not meet its duty under article 145 to take necessary measures to ensure the effective protection of the marine environment. my second question turning to the new proposal for pilot mining after a war of an exploitation contract. we do not consider validation monitoring before commercial production to be an essential part of the process. but our question, like others, is to ask, what if the findings of the pilot mining and the updated environmental plans do not meet the criteria of draft regulation 13, the proposal seems silent on this most crucial question. would the contractor be expected to adjust their approach and try again in the event that the dr 13 criteria ultimately cannot be met by contractors. approach, would the contractor or the contract, sorry, be terminated? we're concerned about the isa is ability to terminate a contract at this stage, or otherwise block a move to commercial mining once the exploitation contract has been given. we also have concerns for how the results of the pilot mining report can be verified independently. we see that there will be zero incentive for a contractor to report outcomes of pilot mining if they're not in their favor, and we remain unclear whether the isa will have any ability to verify environmental data independently, but recognize this is being addressed in other parts of the regulation. a precautionary approach should be taken to test mining, which means the isa should be seeking as much information as it can obtain prior to any first contract award. as a novel industry that is inherently destructive, we really need to get the process right and ensure that all safeguards are in place before we open a pandora's box that cannot be shut. thank you

by the contractor, the authority shall organize and for independent experts to monitor the effects of activities in the area for the first seven years of commercial production, in accordance with the relevant standard and taking into account the relevant guidelines. this independent monitoring program shall be financed by the contractor. the commission shall evaluate and compare the results of comments regarding the 49 in paragraph one, we suggest adding the following words at the end of the provision quote, and shall transmit monitoring data to the authority in real time where feasible, and otherwise monthly, end of quote. we know that this request, that this requirement was included in previous version of the draft regulations, but has been lost in the latest iteration. additionally, we suggest referencing both environmental impacts and environmental effects throughout dr 49 as both have separate meanings in the schedule and both are important in paragraph four, we support the reference to thresholds and suggest adding a reference to the authorities strategic environmental goals and objectives and will provide the text in writing, paragraph five seems to allow a contractor to decide whether harmful effects qualify as an incident or only a notifiable event. we see this as problematic and wish to make a broader point here. environmental monitoring should not only identify harmful effects once they have occurred. instead, the monitoring program should act as an early warning system which alerts the contractor and the authority when there is a risk of harmful effects, so that the contractor can modify operations to avoid those effects. an example here are precautionary reference points used in fisheries management, whereby warning belts go off once these relatively low precautionary reference points are reached well before the fish stocks are over fished. we need similarly responsive thresholds for seabed mining. the threshold working groups could achieve that by developing several thresholds for each impact. for example, a low threshold for noise pollution would identify risks of harmful effect. a medium threshold would identify when harmful effects are caused, and a high threshold for noise pollution would identify when serious harm is caused. these various steps of thresholds would then need to be adequately referenced in the draft regulations. thank you, mister president.
