benefit of all humankind. we find it puzzling that the mechanism through which, in some ways, common heritage principle is to take effect has never been meaningfully discussed in council or assembly reports and proposals have been made from the secretariat to the finance committee and back without any input, suggestions or proposals from isa member states, let alone stakeholders. it appears to us, based on previous finance committee reports, that the finance committee has now settled on the creation of a fund, either as an alternative or in addition to direct distribution to support the work of the isa itself. the report notes a reference to the united nations multi dimensional vulnerability index. the initial proposal for the creation of a fund, as opposed to direct distribution, was based on a model that used gdp per capita as the criteria for calculating equitability if the mbi is now used, which we believe is a good step for factoring in special circumstances of sids, for instance, then the model we assume might look different, and the benefits going to individual countries could change substantially. perhaps the m, v, i index could be introduced to council or assembly, and the new findings analyze collectively, we recall that in previous years, the committee has suggested the fund being utilized towards fulfilling some of the functions and mandates of the property itself. if that remains the thinking, we question whether using the proceeds from mining for the function of the isa isa itself would be a proper realization of overall benefits to human kind, which under the convention is to be used, particularly for the needs and interests of developing countries. we also have some reservations about the legal and practical challenges of the fund being managed by existing organs of the isa. such a structure would diverge from international best practice, where sovereign wealth managed, fund management is typically run by a central bank with significant financial expertise, staffing and experience managing foreign exchange reserves. in contrast, the finance committee the isa has 15 members, none of whom are full time employees of the isa, nor appear experienced in asset management for a large fund. we note that the finance committee recommends that the secretariat be tasked with a report and a concept note to develop a report on this fund. however, without discussion of the fundamental aspects of the benefit sharing regime in council or assembly, we consider this task of the secretariat to be both premature and impractical. i'm concluding we therefore urge members to urgently discuss this crucial part of the regime in depth, first, perhaps on the basis of the reports that have been considered by the finance committee in recent years as a basis for discussion, and then policy direction given to the secretariat to undertake any further steps. in this regard, we support the need for council, or as brazil has just column5: thank you, mr. president, for giving me the fuller and for moderating this discussion. there were a lot of interventions, and i've been taking notes, and i have them grouped in a number of categories. let's deal with some of the easy ones, like on the audit and costa rica ireland, if you mentioned the possibility of using un auditors, as opposed to calvert gordon. the majority of delegations seem to support our finding that as a competent and reliable auditor, that, based on our tendering process and financial responsibility, we had come to select calvert gordon for the last and for the next audit period regarding the un as a possibility. and maybe i've been here a long time and have the corporate memory, but a lot of and this and a lot of the other issues that were raised as if they were new, were actually issues that were asked and answered and and discussed. for example, the use of un auditors was discussed in the 22nd session. in 2023 i actually pulled up the report it is is 20 is by slash 28 slash a, slash four, is the slash 28 slash c, slash 13, and in paragraph 11, i'll read it out. the committee acknowledged with appreciation that the secretariat had contacted the board of auditors of the united nations, as requested by the committee in 2022 it was noted that the rate provided by the board of auditors was $38,820 for the year, and so for each year of 2023 and 2024 with additional travel charges, round trip, air tickets, daily subsistence allowance for the assigned auditors, which i think was a minimum of three, doesn't say that here, which was substantially more than the currently budgeted cost and significantly higher than other bids received. so $38,820 i recall that the audit cost for that year is 19,000 so $38,820 is the fee, and then the air tickets, and then the dsa, which right now is, i think, 500 us dollars a day. and i it's not here, but i think they needed a minimum of three weeks to a month. so we could not accept that something i we didn't do a full costing of all those additional things. i think the 38,000 which was double what, what, whatever the auditor that we chose that year was, was already enough to eliminate that option for this round. i believe they didn't even respond to our request for un orders. didn't even respond to our request for yeah, they didn't even respond. so we didn't even have a cost figure, but i think they knew that they wouldn't be selected because of probably three to four to five times more the costs and in this day of fiscal restraint and the adherence to zng, i think that's not it was. it was eliminated, but we could look at that if, if again and do a more detailed analysis for the next round to show on, on the contractors cost, there was support from tonga and uk and canada, and we appreciate that we took tonga's advice in advance, not not knowing that tonga would also agree to this, but there are members in the finance committee that did advocate for a delayed imposition of the new fee to allow for budgeting, and that's why we chose january 1 2027 so thank you for that. and as canada noted, if those fees don't come from the contractors, then they'll come from you in the form of higher assess contributions. on the question of meeting length, we are aware and also on virtual participation. i guess i could touch on that a few delegations. i'll thank them afterwards. uk, france and ghana recommended longer meeting periods for the finance committee. but seriously, we did find that three days for a non budget year is already tight, and we do know that it will take longer in the past. i think we went to four days in budget years, but i i am previewing that that might not be enough to and i've already been talking with the secretary about looking at more webinars, informal and virtual participation webinars throughout this coming year to explore all the different issues with the budget. i'm for seeing a very difficult discussion because of all the added functionalities that the secretary is being asked to do, possibly the epc inspectors doing cumulative effects, studies in science that the ltc wants to do, and a whole host of new functions that the secretary will have to do to remain fit for purpose and being constrained by zero nominal growth. i think that is actually inconsistent with the treaty. the 1994 agreement does say that we have to use an evolutionary approach. so we'll have to consider evolving the secretary the isa into a full blown regulator of exploitation activities one day. and so it will be a very difficult decision to increase our budget substantially to be able to do all functions that we're being asked to do. and meeting length, i think a good compromise would be to do more online, virtual meetings in the lead up to the final in person meeting in july. so we do anticipate spending more time meeting, but mostly virtually, to keep costs in control on i think those are the easy ones. now on the fun. i think the many countries that supported our recommendation for the secretary to do more study on the concept of the fund sierra lonely for the africa group, nigeria, canada, ghana, canada, tonga, portugal, morocco, singapore, italy. i thank you all for your support. i really thank france for its mention of best practices in multilateral the multilateral environment. bbnj uses a fund to distribute the money. i looked at the conference the convention on biodiversity. it received, i think, 380 6 million of donor money, and selected to date, seven very worthy funds to do projects, or seven very worthy recipients to do projects that help achieve the objectives of the convention on biodiversity. and i think there are many more examples where limited resources that are meant to do something good are distributed via a fund mechanism, rather than direct distribution handing them cash. i don't know that the objectives of the conference convention on biodiversity would have been achieved by handing cash to different countries. so that said, i note that some delegations insist that a direct distribution might be the best way. we did have that discussion within the finance committee, and this study does not preclude or eliminate that option. remember, this is a study. this is not a final product. this is a study to look at what the concept of the fund could be, and the concept could involve a mix of direct distribution and projects. so we aren't closing any doors. we are, but we would have closed doors if we would have went with a direct distribution, because then the money is gone to the countries, and it's beyond any kind of oversight. i recall many years ago, it was actually at a pew workshop on us in moon palace, and my brother tembili from the south african delegation, and i had a great debate on the floor that the session was about the distribution of benefits, and we agreed that the isa would not be discharging its obligations to argot pardos, conceptualisation of the common heritage of humankind by doing a direct distribution, because that does not touch on argot pardo concept of intergenerational equity in order to ensure that we have international, inter generational equity to compensate future generations for our using of the resources today, which they won't be able to use in the future. the money, the royalties, the benefits that we collect, must be done in a way that ensures enduring benefit to those monies. so timberly agreed with me that that and i see that the africa group also agrees that having a fund to decide how to distribute that money in a way to achieve all of our objectives is important now again, that may include a mix of direct distribution, but we are not closing the door on that. and members of the finance committee were a microcosm of this debate here. some did feel that direct distribution can't be eliminated, and some even give submitted formula, and that's in the report, submitted formulas that could be alternates. now we talked about the mbi, and i think pew mentioned that as well. we didn't create formulas with just the gni and just the mvi. we took all of those things into account. gdp per capita human development index population. and i keep inviting people to look at technical study. 31 it's hundreds of pages long, and it goes through this analysis, and it shocks me that this is like a new thing that we have to consider. we have to calculate what the benefits will be. it's there. i requested the secretariat to take the very complicated, multi page report with lots of formulas and math in it, and convert it into a interactive tool where you can plug in an amount of money and then see all the countries, what all the countries receive based on the different formulas we have. now, that tool hasn't been updated to include the mvi, because at the time that that tool was done, the mbi wasn't completed yet, but all these other factors are there, and you can see, and it was the conclusion of the finance committee, that none of those formulas are really good. it the disparity, and i invite you all to look at it. it's on the finance committee's website. at the bottom, there's a link. i don't know if we'll be able to get the mbi numbers added to it. but i guess a last point on the fund methodology is that i think there's some misunderstanding among some people to think that this has anything to do with a sovereign wealth fund like norway that, again, was asked and answered many years ago, we have no intention of taking that money and putting in the bank. norway, for instance, has that objective, and it's great for norway to have that money and the interest from it to sustain themselves. we do not have any intention of doing that was eliminated many years ago. when we say fun, we mean a fund to do projects that achieve the objectives of the convention and the 1994 agreement, just like one for cbd, just like the one for bbnj, we're not collecting this money and living off the interest. that's absolutely not the case. so and also on that governance of that fund, that's one of the areas of study. how could that fund be managed in a comprehensive way, obviously, not a 15 member committee that meets once a year in person. it will mean a professional and fully developed governance system modeling the best practices of other funds that handle large amounts of money. on the topic of amounts of money, i remind delegates that are having the finance committee consider the amounts. that's not within the remit of the finance committee. the 1994 agreement stipulates to sleep. it stipulates what the obligation of the finance committee is, which is to develop the rules rps for the distribution of economic and other benefits from activities in the area. we are not the ones that will set the royalty amounts or to set the rates. that's that's the ltc and the council. so we can't we can estimate, and we can guess. we can make hypothetical analysis, and that's what the tool on the on the website does of how much money we'll have, but on that topic, we did discuss that if the amounts are small in the hundreds of 1000s or millions, even having a direct distribution will mean might like very small amounts of money, and that isn't something that we want to distribute. it just wouldn't make sense for this for us to distribute. you know, $550 to a state park to a member, and so the idea of holding that money in a fund until the amounts are worthwhile to either distribute or do projects was something that we had very early on discuss my dear friend eden charles and i were in a workshop in 2012 to talk about how to handle now, in this case, it was benefits from article 82 but that as early as 2012 many of the many of the colleagues that looked in detail at this subject and how the math would work out. also determined that having a fund that does projects of regional benefit, rather than handing small amounts of money to different countries, was a way to achieve the objectives of the convention and the 1994 agreement. so i want to assure any, any members in the council, in the assembly, that this is not a final decision. this is, like we said, development of the concept of the fund. so we're not developing the fund, we're developing the concept, and we're trying to be informed on what the governance cost would be, what the criteria could be, and whether direct distribution might be part of the mix. so i thank everyone for their comments, and you can look forward to more work from the finance committee on this. again, we've been working on this since 2012 and to pick a direction that doesn't limit options was very difficult, and this, i think, this way forward of of keeping our options open and yet investigating ways in which this can happen is a is a good compromise of all the views that were in the finance committee as well as in the council.

column5: kindly allow me to take this opportunity on behalf of the people of republic of south africa and the international community to the to honor and celebrate the nelson mandela international day. dr nelson mandela was born on 18 july, 1918, in the village of invenso, of vessel in the eastern cape in south africa. and today would have been the 100 and seventh birthday celebration of a man who meant so much to so many people, mr. president, like many south africans, nelson mandela shared a great love for nature and protection of the environment, where, in he pioneered environmental rights for all citizens to be enshrined in our constitution, and which provides under section 24 of our constitution that everyone has the right to an environment that is not harmful to their health or well being, and to have the environment protected for the benefit of the present and future generations and secure ecologically sustainable development and use of natural resources while promoting justifiable economic and social development. mr. president, under the context of the exploration and potential exploitation of mineral resources found in the oceans, and taking into consideration current issues that we are faced with, i would like to quote two important paragraphs from nelson mandela speech presented on the 11th of november 1997 at the fifth session of the independent world commission on the oceans held in cape town, which reads as follows, i quote, the law of the sea treaty recognizes that the wealth of the oceans is part of the common heritage of humanity, yet without a regulatory authority or enforceable law, alarming threats to the oceans face us because of such practices as the dumping of toxic waste over fishing or transnational crime like drug trafficking, the efforts to establish a workable legal order for the oceans must not fail, close quote, but significantly, nelson mandela continue to express that i quote. we do all know that there are no easy solution. we have to strike some difficult balances in the use of the oceans. close quote, mister president, these days an opportunity for the people to recognize their individual power to change the world for the better. and i hereby invite the international community present today, including the international organization, to also play an important part by raising awareness and expanding the reach of mandela's values, including the fight against injustice, helping people in need and advancing reconciliation.

column5: mr. president, i thank you for the opportunity to share our perspective on a topical issue of significant concern to member states of the authority. let me firstly thank the president of council for his statement, which has provided some clarity on issues of concern to countries like mine. sam moore, i also acknowledge the commitment and hard work of council members during this 30th session, mr. president, we are in times of uncertainty and turbulence. multilateralism is under attack and international law is being discarded. samoa, as it sits, is acutely aware of the importance of the ocean to both our livelihoods, continued prosperity and survival. the global voice on this matter was loudly amplified and convincing during the un ocean conference, in nice to this end, we recognize the critical importance of the three pillars of our ocean that deserve full and unwavering attention the health of the ocean, its governance founded on the principle of multilateralism, cooperation and the rule of law, and finally, the sustainable and effective management and use of its resources. we strongly believe mr. president that all three pillars are linked to the current negotiations. what is required is a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework that includes environmental standard, operational guidelines, monitoring protocol and enforcement mechanism. without such guidance, it will be impossible to authorize or indeed monitor any commercial deep-sea mining activities in november 2023, many countries in this room signed the european, african, caribbean and pacific agreement, now officially called the sao agreement. it's a comprehensive mix agreement with a life span of 20 years. mr. president, i want to quote a paragraph from that agreement, which was endorsed and signed by 106 countries on the issue of dc mining. and i quote the parties recognize the general concern raised about the impact of seabed mining on the marine environment and its biodiversity, they shall use the best available science, apply the precautionary principle and ecosystem approach, promote research and share best practices in field of mutual interest to seabed mineral resources in order to ensure the sound environmental management of activities for the protection and preservation of the marine environment and its biodiversity. mr. president, it is clear to my delegation that at this juncture of our consideration of the matter before us, the scientific evidence to assure us that the marine environment will be protected from the harmful effect of deep-sea mining is not fully available, nor conclusive. the rest are too great for us to do otherwise, but to pause until we are satisfied that exploitation activities can proceed without risking significant harm to our marine environment. second, the proposed rules, regulations and procedures are our piece must align with the relevant provision of unclos, for they are essential to governing activities to be undertaken by contractors and provide for the equitable sharing of financial and economic benefit derived from such activities without these are peace, there is no legal basis for authorizing or overseeing commercial deep-sea mining activities. mr. president samoa caution that in our haste to address one challenge, we do not create an even worse problem for ourselves. finally, from current discussion, there is a need to be clear about the institutional capacity of the authority through its legal and technical commission and the secretariat to perform its mandated role with respect to scrutinizing application and ensuring compliance with the rrps and the terms and condition of contract for the above reasons, mr. president samoa, alliance itself with france and other member states who have called for a moratorium or precautionary post on deep-sea mining exploitation. i thank you.

column5: costa rica wishes first to express its recognition and gratitude for the work carried out by members of the finance committee, as well as for the clarity of the report that has been presented was explained by the president of council, has an additional and non negligible cost. however, the benefits of an audit will not only mean whatever the cost of it is, an audit carried out by the united nations will consist in a much more comprehensive review that is of great importance, as we are at the beginning of a new administration with the current secretary general. and in this regard, transparency an institutional trust will be strengthened if that audit is carried out. for this reason, we reiterate our request, mr. president, and that this be carried out, mr. president, allow me to also refer to the request made in council by my delegation about the development of mechanisms for the sharing of resources from activities in the area. the equitable distribution of resources is not a secondary aspiration, but rather a indispensable and essential prior element, element that must essentially be carried out prior to any activity in the area. in keeping with the spirit and the letter of article 140 of the commission, the finance of the convention, the finance committee, must carry out a proactive role in formulating proposed regulations that would allow for the equitable distribution of benefits, according to the mandate of article 140 and this and must carry out its support for council on the different alternatives that could be developed to comply with this mandate, it is within the council's jurisdiction to determine which alternative is the most convenient. we are concerned that the committee appears to privilege almost exclusively the creation of a common fund fund as the sole mechanisms for the distribution of benefits when there could be other alternatives that should have been taken into account and appear to have not been explored or about which we have not yet been apprised by the committee. we recognize the usefulness of a common fund is one of the possible options. we insist there must not be the only one. likewise, the determination of an alternative, the choice of one alternative or another, is a decision that must be left only to the member states. and to decide responsibly about these alternatives. we need specific information about these various alternatives. my delegation, for this reason, considers that the debate about different alternatives is something that must happen, both within council and within the assembly, as where many of the countries are present who are interested in the distribution of benefits in council. we have also repeated on a number of occasions some preliminary estimates which would suggest that under certain royalty schemes, the benefits for the states could be under $100,000 annually. and in fact, mr. president, even much lower amounts when this matter was addressed in council. this creates a legitimate question, mr. president, what amount is the minimum amount necessary and which will justify the threat to the common heritage of humankind. we need to know as council as well as the assembly, what is the amount that states parties would expect to receive once activities in the area are carried out, in order to make to take that decision and whether or not it is worth to undertake activities with all of the risks that these involve, we would expect that a undertaking activities that would represent such a threat, should allow at least an improvement in the quality of life of persons. otherwise it would not make sense. and for this, we must have specific information, not only with a fund as a single channel for the distribution of resources, which would not really allow us to understand how much would be paid to each state and what the true benefit would be, mr. president, this matter has not been sufficiently addressed or discussed and has been subsumed in technical or administrative considerations. we propose that it be included as a specific agenda item for council and of the 31st session of the of the assembly, with sufficient analytics support by the finance committee, we also request that, in its capacity, the finance committee, as a subsidiary organ of council, develop comparative models for the distribution of benefits based on different royalty schemes.

administrative instruction that is is va slash, st slash, ai slash 2023, slash three, slash, amend, dot two was published in january 2025, amending the procedures for classification and reclassification of positions so that the secretary general may directly authorize the reclassification of a position as a result of restructuring without requiring prior submission to standard classification and reclassification of positions is not in line with the decision of the assembly, we respectfully request confirmation that the decision of the assembly will be fully respected and implemented over what is set out in the amendment. secondly, we are concerned that the finance committee was unable to reach a conclusion on the legal framework and condition of the recent restructuring of the secretariat. we hope that the finance committee could share their considerations in this assessment. and finally, we know that at the request of the finance committee, the secretariat, had provided an overview of potential financial scenarios with regard to the ongoing litigation before the joint appeals board and the un appeals tribunal. without prejudice to the confidentiality of these cases, we request for the potential financial scenarios to be shared with member states for our information, including potential legal costs and financial liabilities that the authority may incur in the event of unfavorable decisions. many other delegations have also made similar requests, and they are grounded in the spirit of transparency and accountability, which is important to the isa, which we believe to be a principle and rules based organization.

column5: firstly, allow me to congratulate you and the co chairs on your elections. you have pew support. thank you too. to madam secretary general, her staff and our host, jamaica. i'd like to also thank the finance committee and the chair for their work in the report assembly members, one of the cornerstones of the regime for exploitation in the area is the equitable distribution of the financial proceeds for the benefit of all humankind. pew finds it puzzling that the mechanism through which, in some ways, the common heritage principle is to take effect has never been meaningfully discussed in council nor assembly. reports and proposals have been made from the secretariat to the finance committee and back, without any substantive inputs, suggestions or proposals from isa member states, let alone stakeholders. it appears, based on previous finance committee reports, that the finance committee has now settled on the creation of a fund, either as an alternative or in addition to direct distribution to support the work of the isa itself. we take note of the chair's remarks this morning that the finance committee has contemplated many different models for direct distribution, including using gdp, gni per capita and population, and recently the multi dimensional vulnerability index to calculate the amounts of benefits that each country might receive under various models. we also heard that based on these analysis, the finance committee has come to the conclusion that a fund would better serve the interests of member states. mr. president, in our understanding, the initial proposal for the creation of a fund, as opposed to direct distribution, was based on a model that used gdp per capita as the criteria for calculating equitability. if the m v i is now used, and we believe this is a good step for factoring in special circumstances of sids, for instance, then the model might look different, and the benefits going to individual countries could change substantially. turning to the proposal of the common heritage fund, we have reservations about the legal and practical challenges of the fund being managed by the existing organs of the isa. such a structure might diverge from the international best practice for fund management. while we understand that some of these issues have been analyzed in the reports made to the finance committee and might be available on the isa website, we take note with concern that neither the council nor the assembly, has ever had a proper opportunity to discuss these reports in depth. we note the finance committee recommends that the secretariat be tasked with a report and a concept note to develop a report on this fund, absent a discussion of this mechanism within council or assembly. we fear this ask of the secretariat would be both premature and impractical. therefore, we urge members to urgently discuss this crucial part of the regime in depth, first, perhaps on the basis of the reports that have been considered by the finance committee in recent years, and then provide policy direction to the secretariat to undertake any further steps. in this regard, we support the need for the assembly to discuss this crucial matter as a stand alone agenda item at its next session. thank you for your attention.

column5: the secretary wishes to update. provide a brief update on the status of the pending cases before the joint appeals board and the appeals tribunal. we hear the concerns regarding the possible financial implications of the ongoing litigation, and we wish to state at the outset that the joint appeals board's role is to provide a decision as to whether or not the contested decisions are lawful, and it does not have the power to potentially award financial compensation to appellants, and that authority lies with the un appeals tribunal. and currently there are five pending cases before the joint appeals board. there are also three motions for interlocutor relief before the un appeals tribunal. the joint appeals board has not yet ruled on the five pending cases. the appeals tribunal, however, has ruled on one motion for interim relief in favor of the authority. additionally, the joint appeals board has not ruled on whether four of the five appeals filed by non staff members are receivable in our submissions the authority requested or challenge the receivab ability of four of those applications, and requested that the joint appeals board provide a ruling on the receivability of those applications. as far as remedies, i was concerned, all appellants have requested a rescission of the administrative decision on appeal, and as i said earlier the outset, the joint appeals board has not, does not have the authority to award financial compensation to the appellants. it may, however, find in favor of the appellants, and as a relief, award a rescission or order rescission of the contested decision. if that decision is appealed by the authority before the appeals tribunal, one of the remedies open to the authority is to request payment in lieu of rescission, which is provided for under the un appeals tribunals statute, and i have no further updates on it, but that's an update of our current cases before the joint appeals board and appeals tribunal.

column4: deep-sea is not a barren wasteland; interconnected ecosystems; we rely on a healthy ocean for survival; in our haste to solve one problem, we should not rush to create another one; unclos does not require a deadline; the knowledge landscape around deep seabed mining is riddled with gaps in science, in governance and in participation; directly calls out tmc lobbying; this crisis was not created by states, but by corporate interests; pacific states are not sponsoring out of greed, but out of desperation; deep-sea mining poses irreversible risk to ocean health, the climate and human rights; un scientific advirsory board warned dsm is high risk, high uncertainty, low reversibility; if un says pause, why do we rush?; calls for general policy; article 145 is not optional; gatekeeping going on; scientists, indigenous leaders and civil society must be included; the interconnectedness of of the ocean mirrors that of pacific cultures; indigenous people and local communities must have formal input; palau wants to build the trust in isa, this is important; is this the legacy we want to leave our children?; moratorium: we are not calling for a delay in progress, we are calling for wisdom
column5: thank you, mr. president. as this is the first time i'm taking the floor during this assembly, i would like to express palau's gratitude to you for guiding our work. i also wish to acknowledge the report of madam secretary general and affirm palau's full support for your leadership and stewardship of this august authority center appointment. let me take this opportunity to thank our gracious host, the government and people of jamaica for your warm welcome and generous hospitality on this beautiful island. excellencies, colleagues and friends, it is my honor to address the assembly here today on behalf of a big ocean state, large in resolve and unwavering in our commitment to protect the common heritage of human kind. today, we once again stand at a decision point that will define the fate of our shared seabed, the largest living space on earth and our largest carbon safety, as i have reminded the world many times, the deep seabed is not a barren wasteland, but a vast, vibrant realm that stabilizes our climate, feeds our fisheries, and is home to ancient and unknown life forms once disturbed, it cannot be restored. we now understand enough about the deep ocean ecology to know that deep seabed mining poses significant environmental risk to fragile, interconnected ecosystems that help sustain all life on our planet. if mining commence commences, it could have far reaching consequences, especially for coastal communities like palau, who rely on a healthy ocean for survival. the area lies in the pacific ocean in our very backyard. it is our waters and our peoples who feel the potential, potentially devastating environmental impact. first, in short, exposing the sea, exploiting the seabed, is not a necessity. it is a choice, and it is reckless. it is gambling with a future of pacific island children who will inherit dire consequences of decisions made far from their shores. for years, deep seabed mining has been marketed as green, but in reality, it is soaked with risk and deception. last year, when i addressed this assembly, i said, in our haste to solve one problem, we must not create another, even larger one. this year, the evidence is clear. we are already moving in the wrong direction. we are rushing to prepare regulations atop a foundation of scientific uncertainty, in direct contradiction of our obligation under article 145 of un cost to protect the marine environment. but we must ask ourselves, what is driving this urgency to complete the regulations? the timeline identified by the council in 2023 was only indicative. it was never binding and should not override our duty to act with care. this is not urgency born out of science, but exhilaration shaped by external pressure. we must be guided by principle and not by artificial deadlines. un cost does not require a deadline for a mining code, what on cost does require is that we uphold its principles using the latest science wisdom and legal clarity to guide us. independent science tells us we are at least a decade away from the knowledge we need, and with over 30 core regulatory issues unresolved, fast tracking decisions risk hollowing out this authority's credibility. let us face the facts. we are simply not ready. when this authority was established in 1994 we knew little about the potential harm of deep-sea mining. we hoped it might bring shared wealth to all. but now we know better. mining the seabed will leave behind a shared ecological debt so vast our children would pay the price for lifetimes. it is not a deposit into the future. it is an overdraft against the planet's life support system. the knowledge landscape around deep seabed mining is riddled with gaps in science, in governance and in participation, too often, these gaps are prepared paper over with processes that favor the well resourced and for small delegations like palau, the pace and structure of negotiations driven by manufactured urgency to finalize regulations make meaningful participation an uphill battle. this is not inclusive governance. it is selective exclusion. for years, one company, the metal company, the metals company lobbied this authority to fast track exploitation, promising riches to small island developing states like mine, and huge returns to investors. these promises have proven false, now, having failed to gain legitimacy, tmc seeks to mine unilaterally, invoking a domestic law that has been widely discredited under international law. this is legal exceptionalism and an assault on multilateralism. let us be clear, the crisis was not created by states, but by corporate interests. palau therefore renews its call, joined by 37 states for a moratorium, precautionary pause, or ban on deep-sea mining in this area. and we must acknowledge this inconvenient truth that some of our pacific brothers and sisters are considering mining not out of greed, but out of desperation, a loss and damage. climate finance is loss and damage. climate finance goes undelivered, and they face the stark reality of living on the front line of the climate crisis and the financial burden and human rights burdens that that entail. they face difficult choices. we must respond with solidarity. we must work together on pathways for alternative financing born from regenerative ocean solutions, solutions that facilitate stewardship over sacrifice. the isa is a un instrument, and the un has 17 sustainable development goals, including sgg, 14 life below water, which palau fought for and championed. i urge member states and the secretariat to recall what those goals were designed to achieve, and to listen to the latest guidance from the un in may of this year, the un special rapporteur on human rights and climate change issued a stark warning, deep seabed mining poses irreversible risk to ocean health, the climate and human rights, they called for a precautionary pause, not as a recommendation, but as a legal obligation. the un scientific advisory board likewise warned that dsm brings high risk, high uncertainty and low reversibility. they also call for a precautionary pause, and we echo those calls if we are here to uphold unclos, how can we justify ignoring this un guidance, if the un says, pause, why are we exhilarating? and let us not pretend to be powerless. every unclos state party has legal obligations. palau will not allow our companies, our nationals are named to be used in violation of international law, and we urge others to make the same commitment. and we cannot press forward with exploitation regulations while sidelining the urgent need for a general policy for protection of the marine environment. palau, alongside chile, costa rica, france and vanuatu championed the proposal in 2023 which is now backed by widespread international support after two years of deliberations, we are pleased to see this critical issue finally reflected on the agenda at this meeting. we thank chile for its continued leadership and tireless efforts in championing this important proposal, and we call on the member states to engage with it in good faith. i want to remind us all that article 145 is not optional. it's an obligation, and the continuous push back only underscores how vital this discussion is as we look to the future of the authority, we urge a comprehensive review under article 154 to modernize its structure mandate and formalize alignment with the bbnj agreement and the coming montreal biodiversity framework we do not operate in a legal vacuum. our decisions must reflect the broader international law, including frameworks on human rights, the rights to nature, indigenous rights and biodiversity protection. yet we continue to sideline the very voices that defend these principles, scientists, indigenous leaders and civil society all have a vital role to play in this process if we fail to include and consult them meaningfully. it's not governance, it's gate keeping in palau our legend of lat migaig, the ancestral our ancestral mother, illustrates the inseparable connection between land and the deep-sea in palau and culture, lat migaig is the origin of all life in palau and the ocean, particularly the deep ocean, is where her descendants reside. this interconnectedness mirrors the reality for many pacific cultures, our ancestors, spirits and future generations are bound to the deep ocean and seabed, making its protection not just an environmental obligation but a cultural imperative. a standing committee under the isa would ensure that cultural heritage is not treated as an afterthought, but it is systematically considered before any deep-sea mining activities commence. this committee should also ensure that indigenous peoples and local communities have a formal role in decision making, particularly through free, prior and informed consent mechanisms when their cultural heritage is affected. palau believes in the potential of this authority, and we do not come to dismantle it. we come to rebuild trust in it. the isa has the opportunity to lead the world by becoming a visionary hub for cutting edge science, ocean discovery, inter generational equity and environmental governance, a place where financing is drawn from regenerative, not extractive sources, where the benefit sharing is built in from the start, not added on as an afterthought, where indigenous knowledge and underwater cultural heritage is not only respected, but fully integrated, and most importantly, a place where the voices of those who depend on the ocean and have protected it for generations are heard, heated and centered. the ocean is not just a resource to pacific islanders. it is our life blood. it is ancestral and it is alive. palau was the first nation to ban modern trawling within our waters, because we understood the devastation it causes. but the scale of strip mining proposed by the clarion clipper zone is unprecedented. the area under consideration is the size of india, is this the legacy we want to leave our children, a lifeless ocean floor stretching across millions of square kilometers that could have cascading impacts on the entire pacific ecosystem and beyond history shows multi cultural, multilateral courage will prevail. we protected the ozone layer, we banned nuclear testing, and let us add the deep seabed to our honor roll. as this authority charts the course ahead, youth are watching and speaking out, they are calling, not only for precaution, but for inclusion. we echo their call, the call of the youth and indigenous voices to be part of the decisions shaping the ocean's future, not observers to it. we also urge our friends across the world to join the growing chorus in championing precaution and rejecting the false urgency. a moratorium is not a delay. it is the only responsible path forward in the face of uncertainty. this is a line in the seabed. we are not calling for a delay on progress. we are calling for wisdom, for science over speculation or guardianship over greed. this is not anti development. it is a responsible stewardship the isa can lead that let us be remembered not as the generation that tore up the ocean floor for short term profit, but as the generation that stood up for the deep, for the planet and for each other, and thank you.

column5: thank you, mr. president. excellencies, distinguished delegates, madam secretary general, thank you for your report. i'm truly honored to be sharing this stage with the president of palau and his wise deeply felt words of advice, wisdom and call for action to this assembly, the republic of panama reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the ocean, to the life that the ocean sustains, to marine biodiversity conservation, to respect for all forms of life on earth, to multilateralism, not imposition, to the united nations convention of the on the law of the sea, unoc, and to this authority which bears the solemn responsibility of acting on behalf of all human kind, not a part of human kind, and not corporate greed. the mineral resources of the area are not commodities to be claimed by might nor governed by the anarchy of first come first serve amongst corporations operating in a legal vacuum that is not our mandate. these mineral resources are by the unequivocal letter and spirit of unclos, the common heritage of all mankind. this means it belongs to everyone, not only those private corporations which have the most money or the fewer scruples, or those who use that money to arrive first, exploit the most or extract the fastest or the most destructively, without any environmental regulation or oversight whatsoever. that is our current situation. there is no oversight or regulation whatsoever, thus an immoral feeding frenzy of modern day commercial pirates operating in the best tradition of anarchy and lawlessness is undoubtedly mr. president, a sure recipe for disaster. we must take a very different path. we must behave in a very different manner. our decisions must rise to the moment, to the magnitude of our responsibility over the high seas and the global commons. we must be grounded not in haste, as the president of palau so eloquently expressed, or on political convenience. we must instead be grounded in the integrity of international law, in sound scientific advice, which we do not have, and above all, in our ethical obligation to protect the marine environment for all present and future generations, not for corporations, but yes, for human kind. panama welcomes the considerable progress achieved during this 30th session of the council and the authority, including important advances such as the establishment of a general environmental harm standard, the design of a compliance committee model and the framework for test mining, the adoption of dynamic working moralities reflects a new momentum, and we commend the spirit of cooperation that has brought us here. yet let us not mistake these modest advances for true readiness to guarantee the survival of the deep ocean and the living beings which depend on the zone for their very survival. a comprehensive mining code is far from complete over 3030, 30 major issues remain a result. who are we kidding? the regulatory architecture we are building is intricate, multi disciplinary, and must be aligned without compromise with the binding obligations set forth in unclos, just again, as the president of palau has so eloquently expressed in this forum. therefore, in addition to new international legal frameworks such as the bbnj wto fisheries of cities agreement and the coming montreal global biodiversity framework, which require that we act strictly with within the commitments established in this binding global treaties so as to ensure that the activities in the area do not undermine the effectiveness of these instruments and their objectives. these international agreements are a response to the unprecedented crisis affecting our planet, and they are blinding to achieve their goals. all institutions and countries have the moral obligation, but also the legal obligation, to act in a coherent and coordinated manner to prevent total ecological collapse. yet still today, the science remains woefully insufficient. still today, the legal framework remains under construction and far from complete. still today, the institutional mechanisms remain in flux, incomplete. thus, still today, in such a context, the greatest risk is not delay. that is why the greatest risk is rushing forward, irresponsibly, without the tools to prevent irreversible harm that is the greatest risk. haste makes waste. we are in a critical moment in time, and this is why panama supports the immediate and urgent adoption of a general environmental policy, not as an administrative add on, but as a prerequisite, prerequisite, a prerequisite to the normative as the normative and ethical foundation of this entire regime. we cannot put the cart before the horse. we need a general environmental policy before we continue along the path of discussing the issue of seabed mining. this normative the general environmental policy has to be the normative and ethical foundation of this entire regime. again, it must set a compass anchoring the decisions in the authorities mandate, providing legal clarity and enshrining the primacy of environmental protection over any short term industrial free for all. mr. president, madam secretary, panama is very proud to stand alongside the 37 countries that support a precautionary pause, or better yet, a moratorium on deep-sea mining. we do so because we believe the deep ocean is not a frontier to be conquered, devoured and discarded, but rather a legacy to be safeguarded, a legacy to be studied, a legacy to be understood, indeed, as marine scientific research unveils the silent wonders of the ocean abyss, three different groups of organisms that were immediately visible as we turned on the lights. the first are the groups of or the organisms remain completely motionless. these are basically fish that column5: mr. president, madam secretary-general, distinguished delegates as mr. president has just noticed, i have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the delegations of canada, australia and new zealand. we thank the secretary general and the hard working secretariat of the international seabed authority for providing us once again, with a helpful annual report. as coastal states with significant marine areas under our stewardship, we are acutely aware of the challenges facing our ocean. the health of the ocean is under threat. we are confronting multiple crises impacting on ocean health and resilience, including climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss. these are the cumulative effects of unsustainable human activities and anthropogenic impacts the effective protection of the ocean and the sustainable use of its resources is vitally important to each of us. these shared challenges underline our collective need to maintain and strengthen the multilateral framework for ocean governance. we remain wholly committed to working constructively with all states to strengthen multilateral cooperation in the maritime domain and to improving overall ocean governance. while the united nations convention on the law of the sea may still be young in relative terms, it is difficult to imagine a world without it. it protects and empowers us. it preserves a balance of rights and responsibilities, and adherence to it is critical for the continued conservation and sustainable use of the ocean and its resources. it is the cornerstone of ocean governance and establishes the foundation for a peaceful, stable and prosperous maritime domain by ensuring all countries are operating by the same rules with the challenges facing us in the maritime sphere, maintaining the integrity of the convention is more important than ever. to this end, we reaffirm our steadfast support for the convention. we are also steadfastly committed to supporting the institutions established by the convention, of which the international seabed authority is one. we extend our congratulations for yesterday's commemoration of 30 years of the authority. and as members of the authority, we reaffirm our support for the authority's essential and exclusive mandate to regulate deep seabed mining in areas beyond national jurisdiction. we will continue to uphold the principles, rights, duties and obligations of the convention, including part 11 of the convention and the 1994 implementation agreement. as members of the authority, we will continue to negotiate in good faith to ensure the timely finalization of a robust regulatory regime which ensures the effective protection of the ocean before any mining of the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction goes ahead. we reiterate that exploitation activities in the area should only take place pursuant to robust international seabed authority regulations that ensure the effective protection of the marine environment as required by the convention. it is more important than ever that member states conclude this regulatory framework as swiftly as possible. we also appreciate that following the election last year of you, madam secretary-general, the first woman and the first scientist to hold this role, the secretary, is undergoing a period of transition as well. during this pivotal moment, our countries stand ready to support you to ensure the isa operates under the highest levels of transparency, effectiveness and good governance as it delivers on its important mandate. in conclusion, canada, australia and new zealand are firmly committed to protecting and upholding international law and to the full and effective implementation of the convention. we must all work collectively to accelerate action and mobilize all actors to preserve, protect and sustainably manage our global ocean. we must act together to address the pervasive threats to both the ocean and the multilateral maritime legal order. the stakes are simply too high for us to fail in this endeavor.

column5: singapore wishes to express our appreciation to the secretary general and her team for the comprehensive reports on the report of the implementation of the action plan for marine scientific research in support of the un decade of ocean science singapore notes the comprehensive updates and commends the authority on the good progress made. in particular, we are honored to have contributed to the strategic research priorities of the action plan, including by co organizing a site event at cbd cop 16 to advance deep-sea biodiversity knowledge and promote the synergetic and coherent implementation of initiatives relevant to biodiversity and oceans. singapore has also endorsed the authority's call for action on deep-sea science, technology and innovation, and encourages other member states to do the same. we also reaffirm the importance of robust scientific knowledge and understanding of deep-sea ecosystems in the work of the authority, we are heartened that the secretariat has launched an open source repository on the authority's website, which includes scientific reports from contractors. this is on top of the authority's deep data repository, which has been instrumental in the sharing of non confidential data from exploration activities. we look forward to further efforts from the authority to facilitate the sharing of critical scientific knowledge. we are also happy to see the authority's efforts to advance women's empowerment, particularly the see her exceed mentoring program, which i recall held an excellent and informative side event during the march council meeting. it is our hope that the authority will continue to develop robust and comprehensive capacity building programs, in particular to facilitate the meaningful participation of developing states. singapore also reiterates our appreciation for the secretary general's consultative approach that she has adopted in engagement with stakeholders. we note the secretary general's intentional efforts to engage stakeholders, including sponsoring states and contractors to better understand our concerns and priorities. these engagements are very constructive, and singapore will continue to participate in them actively. we also welcome the active participation of the interim director general of the enterprise, mr. eden charles, in the work of the authority, and we are heartened to see him with us today in good health. we thank him for his leadership, and we look forward to the operationalisation of the enterprise, which will play a significant role in facilitating the participation of developing states and activities in the area. mr. president, this is the year in which we celebrate the 30th session of the authority, which is established under the auspices of the convention and the 1994 agreement, and it is vested under these treaties with the exclusive mandate to organize and control activities in the area. specifically, the convention and the 1994 agreement established a legal framework in accordance with which all deep seabed mining activities in the area are to be carried out. they are clear that the authority has a duty to elaborate and eventually adopt rules, regulations and procedures relating to exploitation of mineral resources in the area. we recognize that the council has been taking some time to elaborate the exploitation regulations, given their complexity and importance. singapore has been actively participating in this process in good faith to ensure that the exploitation regulations are sufficiently robust as befits regulating activities that concern the common heritage of mankind. we welcome the good progress made during the 30th council meetings, in particular the completion of the second reading of the consolidated text and dynamic and productive thematic discussions, including via defense of the president initiative. we further note that a subsidiary of the metals company applied for permits under the united states deep seabed hard minerals act of 1980 we hope to have more information about the company's plans, including to what extent their plans might be inspired by the ongoing work in the isa. we also wish to reiterate that the convention and the 1994 agreement affirm that the area and its resources are the common heritage of humankind, a concept so fundamental that it is commonly considered customary international law. no state may claim appropriate nor exercise sovereignty or sovereign rights over any part of the area or its resources. at the same time, states parties should not be undermining the work of the authority, which has been carried out in accordance with the convention and the 1994 agreement. we heard in a statement made earlier yesterday, a reference to gambling to fail to fulfill our obligations under the convention to develop and adopt robust exploitation regulations will be to leave the door open for unregulated exploitation of the mineral resources of the area which the convention and the 1994 agreement sought to prevent, mr. president, this to us would be considered gambling with the common heritage of humankind that there will be no unregulated exploitation in the absence of exploitation regulations, the convention and the 1994 agreement are one package any selectivity in their implementation and any violation of the common heritage principle would risk under mining the integrity of the legal framework for the ocean that is founded upon these treaties, the authority and the rules based multilateral system, this will not be in the interest of any country. singapore reaffirms our position that deep seabed mining should not commence before robust regulations are adopted, in particular, those intended to ensure effective protection of the marine environment, along with our fellow members of the authority singapore, will continue to work on elaborating the exploitation regulations in good faith. these recent developments are a timely reminder for members to continue to work together to expedite the conclusion of the elaboration of the exploitation regulations, and to ensure that the regulator of the seabed has regulations to fulfill its purpose, this is not only our obligation, but the most effective safeguard for the marine environment and the clearest demonstration of our commitment to the principles of the convention.

column4: notes that only one of five mandatory periodic reviews have been made; needless to say we need one now; supports growing consensus for the need for independent scientific work; mentions ijc advisory opinion; reaffirms precautionary pause stance; welcomes deep-sea dialogues; wants more engagement between assembly and council; assembly has an oversight role; tying isa revenue to mining revenue is a dumb idea
column5: mister president, excellencies, distinguished delegates, tuvalu congratulates you, mister president, and you, madam secretary-general, on your appointment. and we thank our gracious host, jamaica, for the warm hospitality. thank you, secretary general, for your insightful annual report. we also congratulate the isa on reaching its 30th anniversary. scientists tell us that 30 is when the human brain is fully developed, a time when responsibility, purpose and obligation converge, and following yesterday's commemorations, this moment should also mark a face of deeper maturity and sharper focus for the isa an opportunity to check and reset bearings for this modern world in that, in light of that, we know that over the last 30 years, only one of the five mandatory periodic reviews has been conducted. needless to say, a comprehensive review is overdue, not only to assess what has been achieved, but to also diligently examine the effectiveness of the current governance model. this is a fundamental matter of accountability, and not just a procedural issue mister president as a large ocean state, tuvalu's identity is inseparable from the ocean. our culture, our livelihoods and our very survival are bound to the life and health of the marine environment. our fisheries are an important economic resource and also the backbone of food security and cultural continuity. in this regard, we are deeply concerned about how potential deep-sea mining activities, especially those that are trans boundary in nature, could affect our blue economy. tuvalu supports the growing consensus for the need for independent scientific work in this space, positioned on the front lines of the climate crisis, tuvalu has consistently demonstrated strong leadership in advancing environmental protection in collaboration with fellow courses members tuvalu played a pivotal role in obtaining the landmark 2020 4e loss advisory committee advisory opinion, which affirmed that an effective regulatory framework depends on having sufficient up to date scientific information about the marine environment. in that spirit, tuvalu supports the development of a general policy on marine environment protection, and it should not delay progress on regulations. this approach places environmental integrity at the core of decision making. yesterday's commemoration coincided with the historic unanimous icj adversary opinion clearly stating that climate change is an agent and existential threat to human life and natural ecosystems, and that climate action to combat it is a matter of legal duty for high emitting states under international law. more importantly, for this assembly, state parties to the unclos have an obligation to adopt measures to protect and preserve the marine environment, including those from adverse effects of climate change, and to cooperate in good faith, mr. president, we reaffirm and suppose our support for the precautionary pause in deep-sea mining. despite growing scientific insight, the deep-sea remains largely unknown, yet scientists know it plays a vital role in the functioning of the planet. it is also known, as we heard yesterday from the deep-sea dialogs report back that mining threatens unique ecosystems were found to depend on mineral rich habitats with some impact likely to be permanent and irreversible. and here my delegation warmly welcomes the deep-sea dialogs and looks forward to its future iterations. but a precautionary report should not mean inaction. work on the mining code and scientific research must advance, and no mining should proceed without robust scientific data to ensure effective environmental protection. we commend the council for its diligent work and for doing most of the heavy lift. however, mechanisms must be established to ensure that non council members are adequately informed and meaningfully engaged, and that includes allowing the assembly to exercise its oversight role with greater effectiveness. finally, it is our view that the isa faces an inherent conflict of interest. it regulates deep-sea mining while also safeguarding the marine environment and tying isa revenue to mining through the benefit sharing model may skew priorities toward exploitation over protection. to prevent this, we must act with strict caution and full transparency. mister president, seabed may be one of the last truly intact parts of the world, of the earth, if we have failed in so many other domains, climate, biodiversity, pollution, let us not fail here. this is our obligation to the common heritage of human kind. let this be the gift that we pass onto the future generations, tuvalu stands ready to work with you all to uphold that promise.

column5: madam secretary-general, distinguished delegates, pakistan is honored to participate in this pivotal session of the assembly, we extend our warm congratulations to you, mr. president, on your election and commend you for successfully guiding the proceedings. we also express our sincere appreciation to the government of jamaica for hosting this important session in the vibrant and culturally rich country whose warmth and hospitality have greatly enriched our experience, mister president, we we express our appreciation and congratulations to the secretary general of the authority for her first comprehensive and insightful report, and commend the secretariat for its unwavering commitment to advancing the mandate of the authority under the united nations convention on law of the sea. as we commemorate the 30th anniversary of the international seabed authority, we celebrate three decades of collective progress in advancing the common heritage of humankind, the regime for the area has been strengthened through broad participation, effective diplomacy and steadfast commitment to unclos and the 1994 agreement, guided by its strategic plan, 2019, to 2025, and high level action plan the isa has delivered tangible results across all pillars of its mandate, mr. president, we reaffirm our enduring and principle commitment to the legal framework established under unclos, especially the cardinal principle that the resources of the area constitute the common heritage of mankind. this foundational concept must remain the guiding compass for all the decisions concerning the governance, use and equitable distribution of the mineral resources of the deep seabed. the secretary general's report highlights the indispensable role of deep-sea ecosystem as carbon sinks instrumental in mitigating climate change. it also underscores emerging threats, including ocean acidification, marine heat waves and anthropogenic noise pollution, which imperil the delicate balance of marine biodiversity. we echo the report's call for strengthening the science policy interface and enhancing strategic environmental assessments. pakistan emphasizes that capacity building marine technology transfer and rigorous environmental safeguards must be embedded as core pillars in any exploitation regime. in light of rapid technological advancements, it is imperative to strategically leverage cutting edge innovations, particularly artificial intelligence, machine learning and advanced remote sensing to enhance the precision, accountability and environmental integrity of the deep seabed mining operations, the deployment of such transformative technologies must be pursued not merely for efficiency, but to ensure robust regulatory compliance, ecological preservation and anticipatory risk mitigation. equally critical is the imperative to equip developing states with equitable access to these innovations, thereby narrowing the technological divide and fostering inclusive science based stewardship of the area, mr. president, we remain gravely concerned by efforts to accelerate the activation of the exploitation regime in the absence of a comprehensive, balanced and internationally agreed regulatory framework. we reform the importance of precautionary approach and reiterate that no application for exploitation should be considered until the authority has adopted a robust and enforceable legal, environmental and financial framework in the exploitation rules and regulations currently being worked upon in the council. this regime must ensure transparency, equitable benefit, sharing and sustainable stewardship of the area in line with the collective interest of all humankind, as underscored in the secretary general's report, the authority legitimate authorities. legitimacy hinges on inclusivity, transparency and consensus driven process. we urge all states to uphold the collective interest of humanity and to resist expedient actions that may erode long term governance integrity. mister president, this assembly convenes at a transformative juncture in global oceans, governance. the international community has achieved a major milestone with adoption of the bbnj agreement. pakistan is proud to be among the early signatories of the bbnj agreement very recently, on 21st july, 2025 our deputy prime minister and minister for the foreign affairs, his excellency, senator mohammed sagdar, signed the agreement at the united nations headquarters in new york. this act reaffirms pakistan unwavering commitment to law of the sea, to inclusive multilateralism and to the sustainable and equitable governance of global commons. we were actively engaged throughout the bbnj negotiation and had the honor of sharing two important sessions of the group during the final phase. we remain fully committed to contributing constructively to the agreements implementation in synergy with unclos and work of the authority, mister president, we also take this opportunity to warmly welcome and congratulate miss leticia carvalho on her appointment as a secretary general authority. it's truly encouraging to see a woman assume such a leadership role her historic appointment as the first woman to lead the authorities a source of inspiration, and we look forward to working with her to advance equity, sustainability and ocean stewardship. we also thank civil society actors for their active presence and valuable contributions during the session. the engagement through side events, experts, dialog and capacity building efforts continues to enrich discussions, promote transparency and support inclusive partner participation, particularly for the developing countries. mister president. in conclusion, as we reflect on the future of the area, pakistan urges member states to preserve the sanctity of the unclos regime, we must prioritize intergenerational equity over short term expediency. the seabed is a trust, not merely a resource, and it belongs to all the humanity, including generations yet unborn. pakistan stands ready to engage with all stakeholders to ensure that the area and its resources are governed peacefully, equitably and sustainably, in the true spirit of international cooperation and common heritage of mankind.

sea, and as custodian and steward of 54% of the world's ocean floor and its resources, by establishing the legal framework within which all activities in the oceans and seas must be carried out, the convention promotes stability of the law as well as maintenance of international peace and security in a difficult international context, it should be recalled that international jurisprudence has long accepted that its provisions either embody or reflect customary international law. greece has always been a keen supporter of unclos, which constitutes an important pillar of its foreign policy and a reference point in its bilateral relations and maritime issues, mr. president, in its 30th anniversary, the authorities at a crucial juncture facing unforeseen challenges, as madam secretary-general underlined in her statement on monday, in an era of geopolitical uncertainty, we must remain vigilant against attempts at unilateral action in the area. the authority has the exclusive mandate to organize, regulate and control all mineral related activities in the area, on behalf and for the benefit of human kind as a whole, and to provide for the equitable sharing of financial and other economic benefits from activities in the area. unilateral acts are not allowed under the convention. article 136 declares the area and its resources as the common heritage of humankind, whilst article 137 prohibits the appropriation of any part of the area or its resources by any state or natural or juridical person. these rules are also part of customary international law and are therefore binding also upon third states at the same time. however, the authority has the mandate and the duty to ensure the effective protection of the marine environment from harmful effects that may arise from deep-sea mining related activities. in our view, in addition to economic benefits from deep-sea mining, the benefits from living ecosystems intact should also be considered in the context of article 140 mister president, we welcome the progress made in the elaboration of the draft regulations on the exploitation of mineral resources in the area during the 30th session of the council, and we are committed to continuing to negotiate constructively in this respect, it should be stressed, however, that the ongoing negotiations are complex and extremely technical and may take more time as the issues at stake call for careful consideration of all the parameters involved. in this respect, we appreciate the decision of the council to adopt a thematic approach and focus its work on key outstanding issues, instead of establishing unrealistic timelines and roadmaps. unclos does not set a time limit for deep-sea mining as the planet faces a triple crisis, climate change, nature loss and pollution, a hasty decision to begin deep-sea mining may have irreparable effects on deep-sea ocean ecosystems. for this reason, greece had joined the call for a precautionary pause on deep-sea mining until scientific knowledge is sufficient to understand the potential direct and indirect impacts of such an exploitation before undertaking deep-sea mining. it is essential that a robust regulatory framework has been established based on scientific knowledge that can effectively protect the marine environment. for the same reasons, we believe that it is essential to establish a general policy of the authority for the protection and preservation of the marine environment, pursuant to articles 192 145 and 160 of unclos, before any plan of work for exploitation is approved, we are therefore looking forward to a substantive discussion on this issue tomorrow, mr. president, turning to the annual report of the secretary general for 222,025 we would like to thank her and the secretariat for this comprehensive overview of the activities of the authority and the progress achieved throughout the past year. we also welcome the report on the implementation of the isa action plan in support of the united nations decade of ocean science for sustainable development greece attaches great importance to the implementation of the mandate of the authority to promote and encourage the conduct of marine scientific research in the area, enhance scientific knowledge and promote deep-sea research and capacity building, as well as to advancing women's empowerment and leadership in deep-sea related disciplines. we are therefore very pleased that our contribution of 50,000 euros to isa partnership fund was used for the successful organization of the first training course on environmental impact assessments for activities in the area at the isa a deep joint training and research center in alexandria last september. we would also like to thank the secretariat for a very interesting and thought provoking side event on future interactions between isa and the bbnj agreement and its mechanisms. one center did fall the bbnj agreement will provide a solid legal activities of isa and the objectives of the bbnj agreement. greece deposited its instrument of ratification of the bbnj agreement last month at the special ceremony that took place during the third un ocean conference. in nice in this regard, we would like to congratulate costa rica and france for organizing an excellent conference and promoting the swift entry into force and effective also be taken into consideration when we're addressing proposals for unsubstantiated, arbitrary timelines for the adoption of regulations before sufficient scientific evidence is available to clearly
