column5: dosi would like to thank the secretary general for her detailed reports. we appreciate the progress made by the authority in the last year, especially with regard to scientific development, information, accessibility and capacity building. we deeply appreciate the authority's initiatives such as the 1000 reasons project, which funds deep-sea species discovery and description in the area. we take this opportunity to reiterate the deep seas biodiversity remains largely unknown and undescribed. for example, it is currently estimated that more than 90% of the species in the clarion clipperton zone remain to be discovered. dosi commends the authority on enhancing the dissemination, accessibility and transparency of scientific data and knowledge, including via the isa website and deep data repository. we note that many improvements to the deep data including the use of darwin's core vocabulary and connections with databases such as the ocean biodiversity information system or bis. the report notes that the deep data repository follows fair principles, findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable. however, the repository could be further improved in relation to findability and usability of environmental data and information. we are heartened to see the secretary's collaboration and cooperation with international scientific and technical bodies such as the bbnj agreement. these types of collaboration are vital with regard to data storage, accessibility, consistency and compatibility, to ensure their most effective use by scientists and policy makers. likewise, dosi appreciates the deep-sea biobank initiative, creating a repository of biological samples from the area, and we look forward to learning more. we hope that it facilitates access to samples and data sharing and creates further collaboration opportunities with the bbnj agreement, we appreciate the secretariat's fact check documents that attempt to synergize key topics related to the marine environment, but we know that at least some of these documents contain inaccuracies we want to highlight and command the first steps taken by the secretariat towards a collaborative review and correction of these documents with appropriate expertise to which dosi has been invited to collaborate. we look forward to seeing the final product and to further collaborative efforts in the same direction, we acknowledge and commend the progress made in the understanding of the impacts of nodule collectors, as highlighted in paragraph 24 but wish to highlight that the results of single, small scale experiments do not provide an accurate understanding of the effects of commercial mining on the marine environment. furthermore, we would like to stress that there is not a single study that validates the discharge of plume models or deals with their effects in the pelagic environment. this is one example of the many knowledge gaps that still remain in the assessment of impacts of deep-sea mining, as we have done before, dosi emphasizes that, based on our current scientific understanding of the ocean, deep seabed mining will result in biodiversity loss and irreversible harm to deep-sea ecosystems, including changes to the functions and services they provide, scientists have just begun to understand biodiversity, ecosystem functions, oceanography, processes and resilience in the areas targeted for mining, with many gaps remaining. thus, the international community is currently not yet in a position to reliably predict the extent and severity of expected impact from commercial mining, including the plumes, contaminant release and toxicity, noise, vibration and light. how this will affect marine life and any direct or indirect effects on ecosystem services such as genetic resources, climate regulation or commercially important fisheries, available tools such as scientific models that can help to predict impact require robust, robust baseline data, they're not yet available, and small scale in situ tests to verify these models only go so far. deep-sea scientific research is majorly unexplored areas, and the incorporation of this new information into best environmental practices takes time. in short, from a scientific point of view, while we commend the authority on the progress made, we're still just scratching the surface on gathering the scientific information required to ensure the effective protection of the marine environment. we know that there is much to be lost. what we don't know yet is how to protect it. it will take the best collaborative efforts to promote strengthen and conduct ocean science.

column5: madam secretary-general, and distinguished delegates for granting observer status to the ocean and us. thank you to the government of jamaica for your kind hospitality the ocean and us champions ocean health for the survival of all living beings. like many here and around the world, the ocean and us is deeply concerned about the rush by some to open the high seas, our shared heritage to deep-sea mining. our world is literally on fire. the climate crisis, nature collapse, escalating tensions and failed leadership are destroying the natural systems that make life as we know it possible. yet some in this body continue to consider the introduction of a new destructive industry to our ailing world, simply because this was part of the mandate entrusted to this organ more than 30 years ago, deep-sea mining is ecocide. we know that deep-sea mining will compound the multiple crisis we face today. science tells us that the damage caused by deep-sea mining will be irreversible on human timescales, that deep-sea mining will wipe out species before they have even been discovered, and that the consequences of deep-sea mining to ocean functions, including carbon sequestration, are not fully understood. how can we be sleepwalking toward our own demise? it seems our instruments are no longer agile enough to meet the urgency of the moment. unclos and the isa were created at a time when neither the climate nor biodiversity crisis were urgent global concerns, when little regard was given to our diverse cultural heritage, our feminine perspectives and indigenous wisdom, when inadequate consideration was given to the collective, the innate, the future and the undiscovered value of the ocean when we did not, and still don't consider the sentience or potential intelligence of life in the ocean, including the deep-sea. when unclos was negotiated, the concept of well being was different emerging from war and famine. security meant sovereignty, growth and material acquisition. today, security means protecting nature for survival, prosperity and well. being with our shared heritage, the high seas and the intricately connected seabed that belong belongs to us all. we have a chance to do things differently, to break away from the extractive mindset of centuries gone by. let us not repeat the mistakes of the past. we must allow the isa to evolve and change with the times, to become a true steward of the deep-sea. the ocean in us welcomes the new leadership of the isa, offering a promise for more inclusive participation of our diverse perspectives, as well as decision making rooted in science, destroying our shared heritage cannot be how we write history, instead of colonizing the deep-sea beyond national jurisdiction, let us celebrate our global commons as a sanctuary for peace, science and collaboration. last month, we saw a renewed sense of urgency from government supporting a moratorium or precautionary pause on deep-sea mining. there are now 38 countries supporting a precautionary pause or moratorium, and this gives people hope the ocean and us and the 350,000 people from around the world that stand with us, as well as over 165 organizations and cultural centers call on states who have not already done so to choose caution. it will show people that we can come together and prevent a disaster from starting, that we dare to protect what belongs to us all.

column4: neither feasible nor necessary; green transition narrative is false; unviable solution to a battery problem that existed 10 years ago; tmcs business model has not been updated to reflect our current reality; less than 20% of life has returned to mining sites from the 80s; calls for minimum 10 year moratorium
column5: secretary general and distinguished delegates, thank you for this opportunity to speak on behalf of the tettora society, a research and conservation organization based in french polynesia dedicated to protecting island ecosystems and our blue climate initiative, which brings together scientists, communities and cultural leaders to address ocean based climate solutions rooted in deep respect for our ocean. the deep ocean is one of earth's final sanctuaries. it's home to complex life forms, critical climate functions, and untold knowledge. mining the ocean floor is neither feasible nor necessary, and it is driven today only by the greed of a few companies and nations. the metals company had claimed their mission was to support green energy, but we do not need deep-sea minerals to meet our clean energy goals, as we and others have amply shown in papers published on websites, battery technology has already moved beyond the need for men or for nickel manganese and cobalt, and the assertion that the ocean holds a treasure of rare earth minerals is clearly not the case. deep-sea mining stands today as technically challenging, highly destructive, financially unviable solution to a battery problem that existed 10 years ago. what is clear is that in the last five years, drill ship day rates and interest rates have doubled. electric vehicle production has quintupled, but the price of nickel has dropped 19% and cobalt 36% indonesia has suspended 1/3 of its nickel production. new caledonia has closed both of its nickel mines. the level of suspended production equals six times tmc total planned production of nickel from the ocean floor. tmc. business model has not been updated to reflect these economic realities. what is clear is the ecological cost. less than 5% of the deep ocean has been visited, photographed or sampled. deep-sea mining would create sediment plumes that will smother marine life over large areas, while acidic and toxic sludge will be dumped from surface vessels killing and contaminating marine life and releasing stored carbon. evidence from experimental mining shows that less than 20% of life has returned to areas mined in 1989 what is collected clear is that companies like tmc have no ethical qualms about disregarding this institution, the international seabed authority, its mandate from the united nations, the united nations convention on the law of the sea, and blatantly disrespecting the voting members of the isa attempting to bypass international norms by seeking license from the united states. this move is contrary to the international law and undermines the global governance system established through the united nations convention of the law of the sea. for decades, the isa has been the sole multilateral body entrusted to manage these resources on behalf of human kind, to bypass this now sets a dangerous precedent, and there is also a deeper cultural and moral issue here. for the peoples of the pacific, the ocean is not a commodity. it is sacred. it holds history, identity and spirit. deep-sea mining threatens the cultural heritage of pacific islanders, a cultural heritage that demands respect. we draw our attention to our website, where we have a petition of island leaders from across the pacific that are beyond calling for a ban on deep-sea mining taken collectively, everything that i have said argues for a precautionary pause. we urge the isa not to submit to the pressures of companies such as tmc to hastily approved mining licenses. there is no urgency at this time. there is no harm in waiting. this is a defining moment in human history. we will protect the deep-sea as a global commons for future generations. we should not allow it to be spoiled for elusive and un certain short term profit the world is watching. the te society calls for a minimum 10 year moratorium. the isa must not approve commercial mining under until comprehensive environmental protections exist and free prior and informed consent is obtained from affected pacific communities. te taro. society stands with pacific peoples with scientists and economists and business people urging caution. let us call for a moratorium. let us defend our ocean.

column4: fears a moratorium will hurt the environment; us goes for dsm out of frustration; after 30 years excuses for delay is wearing thin; politcal decision, not scientific; science will never be enough; the us has a comprehensive precautionary mining code, it claims; the minerals could help billions out of poverty
column5: opes oceani foundation reiterates its thanks to jamaica for its generosity and commitment as the host of the international seabed authority for the past 30 years. and we also extend our compliments and thanks to the madam secretary-general for her comprehensive report. distinguished delegates, the rules based order and multilateralism may be in jeopardy. things could fall apart that pressing fact places a great responsibility on the isa opa sociani foundation does not doubt the good intentions of those parties and ngos which call for a precautionary pause or moratorium on deep-sea mining, but we fear that if they succeed, they'll do tangible harm to both the environment and the credibility of the established world order. we remind them that the eyes of the world are upon the international seabeds authority. this body was mandated to produce a functioning mining code, and in the eyes of some, it is already overdue, frustrated by the delays at the isa the united states of america says it is going to begin deep-sea mining. if this goes ahead, there would be no globally accepted gold standard against which to calibrate the efficacy of its domestic regulations. the same conundrum exists for nation states planning to launch deep-sea mining ventures within their economic exclusion zones. the isa has a choice. it can bolster confidence in the rules based order by adopting soon a functional, environmentally responsible deep-sea mining code, or it can continue, continue to be seen to block delay and to keep the mining code in limbo after 30 years, the excuses for delay are wearing thin. the science, however useful, will never be complete science is a never ending quest for knowledge for its own sake. there is no alt in science. the decision about whether we ought to deep-sea mine or not is a political and moral choice. we already know enough to write an effective deep-sea mining code, as indicated before the usa has what it believes to be a comprehensive mining code, rooted it says, in the precautionary principle, informed by science our modern, high tech global economy is in crying need of secure supplies of the 17 so called rare earth minerals, which, unlike on land we know are to be found in abundant, commercially viable quantities in multiple, accessible locations on the sea floor, in crusts, sediments and nodules, by making so called rare earth metals and manganese, copper, nickel and cobalt available in never seen before quantities, we could boost wealth generation and sustain innovation to create new industries. this would help lift billions of people out of poverty. but there's an equally pressing reason to adopt the code soon. the correct response to the terrestrial monopolization of rare earth elements is not unilateral action. what we require is multilateralism and the fulfillment of every one of the un sustainable development goals for the isa that demands the establishment by consensus of functional, environmentally responsible regulations that make certain the good governance of deep-sea mining in the area for the benefit of humanity.

international lead and zinc study group, which the interim dg attended in order to obtain accurate and timely information on capacities, production, usage, trade, stocks, prices, technologies, research and development and other factors that may influence the supply and demands of metals could be reported back to the cancer. this might be especially useful for the work of the soon to be established economic and planning commission. the african group continues to emphasize the need to further operationalize the enterprise in the step wise approach, as it remains, the principal vehicle for the effective participation of developing states in activities in the area. the african group has taken note of the interim dg update on the preliminary work undertaken since july 2024 to conceptualize a structured and policy driven organizational model for the enterprise we wish, the african group wishes to underscore that as we approach the finalization of the exploitation regulation, the operationalization of the enterprise must move beyond conceptual planning and into tangible, time bound implementation. the enterprise is a critical pillar in ensuring the realization of the common heritage of humankind and its effective establishment. it's central to upholding equity and the interest of developing states under part 11 of the convention. accordingly, we urge that the next phase of work focus on delivering concrete outcomes that demonstrate measurable progress towards full operational capability. this includes, but it's not limited, to the recruitment of dedicate, dedicated technical and legal personnel, the formal establishment of of its internal governance and financial management systems, the development of a strategy for participating, for participation in joint ventures, and the commencement of preparatory work for potential exploration and exploitation activities, the full and timely establishment of the enterprise is essential to ensure equity capacity building and technology transfer as critical elements of the exploitation regime envisioned by unclos. this strategy, this strategic priority, reflects our firm commitment to upholding the principle of the common heritage of humankind in the governance and exploitation of the deep-sea mineral resources. in this regard, the african group supports the full operationalisation of the enterprise as a commercially oriented entity functioning with a degree of autonomy under the general policies of the assembly and the directives of the council of the international seabed authority, the african group remains committed to supporting this process and calls for a clear and measurable road map to ensure enterprise is positioned to discharge its mandate in accordance with the convention and the 1994 agreement. finally, the african group welcomes the continued efforts by the authority and the dedication shown by the interim dg in advancing the operationalisation of the enterprise.

the authority on the conservation and sustainable use of the international seabed area. the fabric of our pacific community is woven through mutual respect, shared advocacy and collective action. convention on the law of the sea. in this spirit, mr. president, in february of this year, pacific leaders, ministers and officials, gathered in suva for the pacific islands forum high level talanoa column5: first of all, we'd like to thank chile for including this item to the agenda, which is un finished business from the 29th session of the assembly and deserves further consideration. in our view, it is entirely appropriate for the assembly to establish a general policy on the protection and preservation of the marine environment. the assembly is the supreme organ of the authority, and has the power to establish general policies on any question or matter within the competence of the authority, in collaboration with the council, article 145 provides an undisputable legal basis for the elaboration of a general policy on the protection and preservation of the marine environment. there will be no overlap between the general policy and the regulations. such a policy will establish the overall plan and the general environmental goals in the area, setting priorities and providing guidance in light of new circumstances and challenges in accordance with the precautionary principle. it will also ensure consistency between the different organs of the authority on environmental issues, and will provide the framework within which all relevant issues will be discussed, including the widespread concerns about environmental impacts of deep-sea mining or moving to exploitation before sufficient scientific evidence is available to clearly demonstrate that such operations will not result in adverse impact to the marine environment. we agree with brazil that the general policy will also align the efforts of the authority with other international instruments and fora, in particular, with the bbnj agreement, which will also be applicable to the area once it enters into force. we are aware that there are different views between the delegations, both on the need and the scope and parameters of a general policy. however, at this stage, we are not considering the adoption of a general policy, but the establishment of an informal intersessional dialog to discuss these issues, including procedural issues. it would be regrettable it would not be possible to agree even on such an initial step. turning now to the revised draft proposal. we are not in favor of the proposed amendments in sub paragraphs a and b of paragraph four of the draft decision, and more specifically, with a reference to paragraph four section three of the annex to the agreement. in our view, the reference in paragraph one section three of the annex in collaboration with the council, does not imply that the process for the liberation of a general policy should be initiated through a recommendation of the council. however, since there is a divergence of views on the interpretation of these provisions at this stage, we would prefer to leave this issue open and do not make any reference to any particular provision in paragraph four subparagraphs a and b of the draft decision, the procedure for the establishment of a general policy will be one of the main issues to be discussed during the intersessional dialog.

preservation of the marine environment. ireland strongly supports this proposal. the assembly is the supreme organ of the authority, and it has the power to establish general policies on any question or matter within the competence of the authority, as long as those policies are in conformity with unclos, considering that one of the main objectives of the convention is the protection and preservation of the marine environment to which part 12 is dedicated, it should not be controversial for the assembly to informally discuss a general policy to give effect to this obligation. in ireland's view, a general policy for the protection and preservation of the marine environment would give effect to the provisions of article 145 of the convention, and would facilitate coordination and harmonization between the provisions of the convention and the activities of the authority. a general policy would also enable consistency and mutual supportiveness between the organs of the authority, while ireland acknowledges that any decision of the assembly to establish a general policy shall be in collaboration with the council. ireland is of the view that the adoption of the draft decision would be consistent with the distribution of powers and functions among the organs of the authority. this decision, rather than establishing a general policy, simply provides time and space for member states to exchange views on the necessity and content of a potential general policy. moreover, the draft decision specifically provides for engagement with the council, consistent with the 94 agreement. various arguments have been put forward by some space states in opposition to this proposal. they suggest that the trespasses into the matters that are the responsibility of the ltc and the council, that it risks distracting from the mining code, that it will prejudice the mining code, and that the exploitation regulations are sufficient to address environmental concerns. ireland does not accept any of these arguments. in any event, these are all issues that can be further discussed within the intersessional dialog, which, i reiterate, does not provide for the adoption of a general policy, merely a process to consider one at a time when the authority is under considerable international scrutiny, when we are moving towards a potential exploitation phase, and when widespread concerns persist about the environmental impacts of deep-sea mining. it would be highly regrettable if this modest proposal were to be blocked once again by some states, such an outcome would call into question the credibility of the authority as a regulator committed to the protection of the marine environment. it would send a lamentable signal to the outside world. not only will the authority not adopt a general environmental policy, it will not even consider it. this is not a good look. ireland urges the members of the assembly to support the draft decision.
